utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm in a position to distribute the extract from the book that the witness read from the overhead projector yesterday. If that could be distributed to the parties and the Court and given an exhibit number. The Court and the witness will recall this was the one where he spoke of sitting in the dock, keeping a chair free for the accused, asking how the accused could send him to The Hague without Bogdanovic, Kertes, Stanisic, Simatovic, Frenki, and others.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 900.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Seselj, because we dealt with this a little bit quickly yesterday, how was it in 1994 - help us - that you could identify as potential candidates for trials at this Court, this accused, Kertes, Stanisic, Badza, Bogdanovic, and Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost, that is just a witty thing. It's a joke. It's -- I was trying to be funny. If he's sending me to The Hague, then I'm going to keep a chair in the dock for him. And then I also mentioned the names of all his political officials. So this is just a political battle before the general public, who laugh, applaud, and consider this to be a good joke. Now you are looking at heated Serbian political life, and things of this nature in it, and treating it seriously. That's impossible. This was just a witticism, and that's how the entire Serbian public took it. I assume that it upset Mr. Milosevic at the time, that it annoyed him, and that was my intention, to annoy him, but it had no other purpose whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what you say. As to the material you produced over the weekend from various books, can I summarise the extracts that you've produced in this way: There were -- you did say things starting in the late 1990s, either 1998 or 1999, to the effect that the French intelligence were involved in or responsible for Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the best of my knowledge, as vice-premier of Serbia, the French intelligence service staged the massacre of Muslim prisoners of war in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second: You produced no -- or you had copied and produced no reference to any of your writings where you say, at any stage, that the things you were saying about this accused in 1993 were false.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I gave you a large number of excerpts from several of my books, and I explained that all of this was said in the heat of a political debate and as a propaganda war was going on. You keep dodging the issue. You don't want to present this to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen to the question. You can point us to -- or can you, please, point us to one of your 60, or is it 80, published works in which you say, well, in 1993, I said all these things that were entirely false about the accused Milosevic. He had nothing to do with sending volunteers here, there, or everywhere. He wasn't in charge. Is there anywhere in your writings that we can find your saying that? That's what we want to know.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, speaking several years later about the things I said against Mr. Milosevic, I'm presenting a general position which includes all of the above. Now, what normal person or serious politician would go into the details yet again? I said it very concretely. The Ceausescu Couple, and then I deny it. I said The Red Dictator from Dedinje and then I deny it. So it's pointless. With a general assertion, I refuted all of it, not by repeating everything I said beforehand. Why would I repeat all of that if, in a general position, I simply refuted all of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have your answer. Thirdly: In all your writings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the answer that there's nothing in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, If we've missed something, I'm anxious to be corrected but that's why I asked the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct. That is not correct. That's not the kind of answer that was given. I said that it does exist in writing. But Mr. Nice doesn't want to recognise it as such. And he doesn't want to show you the excerpts that I gave you yesterday. He doesn't want to show them to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you say that there is an excerpt marked in the books that you handed over yesterday which clearly shows that you were misleading the public in your earlier statements in the early to mid-1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite clearly, it shows that in all my attacks against Mr. Milosevic from 1993 to 1996, were made with a specific objective in mind, wishing to achieve concrete political effects in our conflict. That is to say that they refute a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point is, though, that you've marked such a passage in the extracts that you gave Mr. Nice to copy yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I marked everything. And this is the point. Let me jog your memory: In the Middle Ages, the scholars had a major debate on how many teeth a donkey has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wish you would just answer the question. Are you saying that you marked a passage in one of the books that you gave Mr. Nice yesterday that deals with this question, that deals with a statement where you say clearly in writing that what you were saying earlier was just misleading and was political propaganda, or are you saying it's written somewhere else and we have to go and look for it and find it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it the latter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, everything is contained in the excerpts I provided yesterday. Precisely, that it was political propaganda --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the former. You had marked the passage which makes it clear that you were making misleading statements earlier. You've marked such a passage for Mr. Nice to copy? Is that the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Seven or eight such excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Seven or eight. Great. Now, Mr. Nice, are you going to give us copies of everything that was marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm certainly happy for you to have copies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are they going to be translated in some way?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, of course, we're working on draft translations. I'll redouble the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we could order the translation, and then we'd be able to see exactly what's said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll review the material again this morning, or have it reviewed in light of the answer given, but as I understand the position from the first read, it was pretty well as I asked in the question. We'll look into that, Your Honour, and I'll come back to it perhaps after the break when I see what we've been able to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last question on the material you provided was this: You'll remember that I've been interested to discover from you whether there was any public acknowledgment by the authorities in Serbia of what happened at Srebrenica before the occasion when Erdemovic was interviewed by journalists and those interviews were going to become public. The date of all that is about the 21st of February, 1996. Have you produced in your writings anything that shows acknowledgment by the -- public acknowledgment by the authorities in Serbia of what happened in Srebrenica before about the 21st of February, 1996?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're now changing the subject. From July 1995, when the crime in Srebrenica was committed, until Erdemovic's arrest, I said nothing about it, because I didn't really have any particular knowledge. I heard bits and pieces, but it was not sufficient to speak in public. But this is a period of less than one year. I don't have any information to the effect that the authorities were speaking about it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The simple answer is no, and we will come back to Srebrenica in due course. I just wanted to deal with the documents you produced. Very well. Can we look at a few more things that you said. We'll start with -- this one is coming up. It's an extract from a book of yours, Radicals are for the Village, City and Honest Work, 12th of December, 1993. If you'd look, please, on page 91 of the B/C/S, and we have a short extract from the -- in the English, which is the second of the two marked passages on your page 91.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is this B/C/S that you refer to? I don't understand that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you mean you don't understand the word as applied in this Court or that you choose not to say you understand the word? "B/C/S" is the term used in this Court periodically or regularly for a language spoken in parts of the former Yugoslavia. Did you not understand that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are inventing a new word for the Serbian language. Do you have any linguistic support for the claim you're stating? Please do not insult my language. What exists is the Serbian language and what you're trying to impose is some name called B/C/S, and that is in contravention of all linguistic rules. Please do not insult my people and my language in that way. I speak the Serbian language and that's the only language that I understand. First you invented the Bosniak nation, now you want to invent the Bosniak language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you've been told before it's not for you to determine how questions are asked and answered, and by and large I've been using with you, I think, the words "the Serbian language." But it is the habit in this Court to refer to it as "B/C/S" for terms, I think, of political neutrality. I'm not sure why and I don't mind why. Your observation is, I think, noted. Would you now please turn to page 91 of the document before you, in a language you understand. And will you look at the extract that's marked, and does it read -- the second of the two extracts marked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have a reference to the tab, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it read, speaking of a letter: "The letter was written in Slobodan Milosevic's cabinet. Milosevic called Martic, Hadzic, Bjegovic, and Mile Novakovic and forced them to sign that letter. He did not have to force Hadzic ..."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am asking the interpreter to read the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then you read the original and we'll follow in English in case there's any --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can read it. It's no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You do it, then.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to the journalist's question, which is not referred to here, and it has to do with a press release issued by Milan Martic and a group of leaders from the Serb Krajina that was referred to yesterday here, and then I responded to that by attacking Milan Martic. The journalist is asking me about that letter. We can't see the question here. And my answer to the question is: "Yes. The letter was written in Slobodan Milosevic's office. Milosevic called Martic, Hadzic, Bjegovic and Mile Novakovic and forced them to sign that letter. He did not have to force Hadzic, he signed immediately." Bjegovic is also closely attached to the regime of the Socialist Party and now he is in this Serb Party of Socialists that the regime established in Krajina that has no stronghold among the population but it has direct regime support from here. Mile Novakovic, after these two fiascoes of his, especially the one from September, has his positions highly shaken in the Krajina. They were talking about his removal and everything was prepared for his removal. General Mile Mrksic was supposed to replace his as commander or, rather, chief of the General Staff of the Serb army. In such a situation, he also signed. Milan Martic hesitated. He opposed it for a while. However, as Milosevic presented him with an ultimatum and threatened him, he signed. As soon as he signed, he was bought, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's enough. Now, then, does that passage - and thank you for reading the full part of it, not just the two short passages extracted - does that reflect the reality of the accused's authority over various people, but in particular, over Martic and Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it something you just made up and put in a book?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't just make it up. The truth is somewhere in the middle, and now I'm going to tell you all about it, Mr. Nice. First of all, Mr. Milosevic did have certain influence over these people. More over some, less over others. He did not have to influence some of them, because I had such a hostile relationship with Hadzic that he could barely wait to sign something like this. However, at this point in time what I have as a fact before me that Milan Martic, Goran Hadzic, Bjegovic, and Mile Novakovic, at the height of our clash - that is to say, between the Radical Party and the Socialist Party and Mr. Milosevic - they attacked us personally and the Radical Party. Now, I'm building an assumption. I don't know whether they went to see Mr. Milosevic. I never saw a meeting of that kind. I am just insinuating. I assume that that was done under his influence, et cetera, et cetera. So what I present in public is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's very difficult for us if you speak at that --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not shouting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, is this, then -- shall we just get to the end of the answer. You're building on assumption, you never saw the meeting, you made an assumption that they were under his influence and you wrote this down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my assumption, that it was either Mr. Milosevic's influence or the influence of his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's rather more said at the beginning of that answer, because it said: "I didn't just make it up. The truth is somewhere in the middle. First of all, Mr. Milosevic did have certain influence over these people."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His Honour reminds me that you acknowledge having some influence over these people. You acknowledge that Milosevic had some influence over these people, but as to the balance, you were building on an assumption; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that they went public with a press release against me personally and the Serb Radical Party at the height of our conflict between us, on the one hand, and the Socialist Party of Mr. Milosevic, on the other hand, speaks in itself that they have taken one particular side. Then this Bjegovic, who was president of the Serb Party of Socialists of the Serb Krajina, I am saying that the regime formed it from here. That is an exaggeration. They were established with the support of the Socialist Party of Serbia, although they never had a stronghold there. They never liked the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. The pace is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the interpreters are asking you to slow down. May I ask you, then: You have no specific evidence, then, that Mr. Milosevic forced Bjegovic and Martic to sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't have any proof. But I am trying to discredit them politically by making these insinuations that they were under pressure, and I come out public with that. You understand: They attack me and now I retort: You did it because Milosevic made you do it. So this is a political battle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And as for Martic, you have no specific evidence that Mr. Milosevic gave him an ultimatum and threatened him and then he signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. No. I don't have any evidence. But, as you can see from this text, I'm now insinuating that there are differences among the signatories themselves, trying to sow discord among them. I say Hadzic could barely wait to sign something like that, Bjegovic must be a socialist, Martic was hesitating, he didn't want to sign it, but ultimately he did, and so on and so forth. So I have a front of political enemies before me. Now, in my political tactics, I'm trying to somehow break them up and I'm trying to make a difference among all of them. Like all the things they said about me. You haven't got that before you, because all of that are also fabrications, insinuations, et cetera. So I'm responding to their fabrications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, at the beginning of that answer, when I think you were trying to give us a genuine account of your position and you weren't reflecting your earlier writings, you said that Milosevic's influence varied, according to the person. Now, looking at the way in which you then presented the individuals, can we take it that in your opinion he had a very considerable influence over Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot say now that he had a very considerable influence over Hadzic, because I had had a hostile relationship with Hadzic for years by then, so he could barely wait to speak out against me. And also, he had an influence over Bjegovic, because it was with the support of the Socialist Party of Serbia that the Serbian Party of Socialists in Krajina was established. Milan Martic was my friend previously, but here he clearly opted against me in Mr. Milosevic's favour. You know, political discourse does not always require concrete evidence for each and every detail, as is required in court proceedings. What is said in the heat of a political debate does not have to be identical to what is said in court proceedings. At least, that is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to ask you again to speak more slowly. The interpreters have asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm now in a position where I don't really understand what you're saying, because you started this exchange by saying: "First of all, Mr. Milosevic did have certain influence over these people," and that's the four named. More over some, less over others. And I was just trying to find out which one he had more influence over. Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm telling you: He had the most influence on Bjegovic, because Bjegovic's Serbian Party of Socialists in the Krajina was established with the direct help of Mr. Milosevic's party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you say was his influence over Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in this specific case, Mr. Milosevic's interests to have support in his conflict with the Serb Radicals corresponded with Mr. Hadzic's desire to attack the Serbian Radical Party, because we were already enemies by that time. I don't know what his relationship with Mr. Milosevic was, because I was never present there. You're asking me the impossible, to explain to you the relationship between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Hadzic. And I was in conflict with Mr. Hadzic from 1991 onwards and making only negative statements about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This excerpt, then, Mr. Seselj, is wholly unreliable as to the influence that Mr. Milosevic had over these persons, certainly in relation to Bjegovic. It indicates that he had to force him to sign the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bjegovic? No. It doesn't say anywhere that he had to force Bjegovic. It says that he had to force Martic. Mr. Robinson, it doesn't say that about Bjegovic. I say that he was very attached to the Socialist Party regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, my -- please correct me if my recollection is wrong, but when we, in examination-in-chief, were considering the question of the involvement of other named persons in the indictment in the joint Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. criminal enterprise, did you not say that there was no question of Mr. Hadzic being involved in any joint criminal enterprise with the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it was impossible that he participated in something with me, because we were constantly in conflict. And what I'm saying is that the accused was not in any kind of joint criminal enterprise. But, Mr. Bonomy, there's something else here: When Milan Babic was dismissed, it was Goran Hadzic who was elected the president of the Republika Srpska Krajina. And the authorities in Belgrade considered Hadzic to be a better solution than Babic, and that is a fact. It cannot be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought that your answer earlier had extended to saying there was no question of a conspiracy or joint criminal enterprise or joint action between the accused and Hadzic, and I note now you say that you were never there, so you don't know what the relationship between them was. Anyway, we can move on now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I continue to assert that there was no joint criminal enterprise, absolutely, among the highest-ranking Serbian officials, there was no such thing. And I abide by what I said. However, here I'm demonstrating that the relations between Mr. Milosevic and each of these men was not of the same nature. He was closer to some people, more aloof from others. He treated some more correctly than others. And at the height of my conflict with Mr. Milosevic, I said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I have one question to put to you on this passage, and it's to reflect the Prosecution's case. Mr. Seselj, when you give the sort of detail that you give in this passage, discriminating between one individual and another, you're revealing that you're actually speaking on this occasion the truth, from which you now seek to hide by lying to this Court. That's our case against you as a witness. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your case is false. I am saying here that I was attacking the signatories of a communique and of course making insinuations to a certain extent. There is something called the symbolism of political discourse. When one says "in Mr. Milosevic's office," it doesn't mean in his office literally. It means under his influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this document be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can it be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd look now, please, at a different exhibit. It's an existing exhibit. It's Exhibit 326, tab 11, a map of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, admitted through Babic, Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If a copy could be handed to the Court and then to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still haven't got a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a copy on the overhead projector. Perhaps you'd be good enough to look at that. That will be screened for you. If the usher would stay there, because I want him to do something for me in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first and very general question is this: Looking at the borders of the Republic of Serb's Krajina, do they resemble or do they fit, to some degree, closely with the appropriate part of the border of the Greater Serbia for which you have always contested? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can't say that it corresponds to the borders of Greater Serbia. The western border of Greater Serbia is the Karlobag-Ogulin-Virovitica-Karlovac line. However, this border is a little to the south of Karlobag, a lot more to the south of Ogulin. No, you can't say it's similar. What is the key difference? Formally, you can say that the western border it's similar. All of Central Slavonia is included in our ideological project of a Greater Serbia, and Slavonia was not part of Republika Srpska Krajina. In our ideological project, there is no gap here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Usher, would you be good enough now, please, to hand the map to the witness and place on the overhead projector the English document, which is the key on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the key and just parts of it, we see that on this map -- this is a map of Ustasha genocide on the people of Serbia on the territory of the Independent State of Croatia, between the year 1941 and 1945. That's one of the inserts, I think. There's a reference to the German representative inviting the Ustashas, stating that a million Orthodox Serbs, children, women, and elderly, have been slaughtered. Then we see reference points to points of genocide committed by Ustasha, mass genocide on the Serbian people, and so on. All these things marked on a map published at the time of the existence of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. Do you accept, Mr. Seselj, that focussing people's attention in the 1990s on these historic, tragic events, but historic events, served a purpose of inciting people to violence?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there's a forgery here. It wasn't the Ustasha who killed the people of Serbia. It was the Serbian people who had lived for centuries on the territory of the so-called Independent State of Croatia. That is an anti-Serb forgery, a major one. It's here at the beginning of this paper. Secondly, until the year 1990, until the fall of Communism, the opening of Serbian mass graves from World War I had been prohibited. It was only when the nationalist parties won in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslim Party of Democratic Action, the Serb party, the HDZ, it was only then that conditions were created for the pits and other mass graves to be opened and given a properly burial to the remains of the Serbian civilians killed in World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: After that background and contextual information, would you please answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: World War II, not I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Answer it directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990 and 1991, Serbian mass graves from World War II were opened in order to give the victims a proper religious burial. That was the only reason. It wasn't a part of preparations for war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll put the question that Mr. Nice put to you, which is whether you accept that focussing people's attention in the 1990s on the historic, tragic events in the 1940s served the purpose of inciting people to violence. I've allowed you to set the context -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I had to supply this explanation, Mr. Robinson, because without it my answer would not have been complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I allowed you to do so, but at a certain time we must get the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you feel free, Mr. Seselj, to speak whenever it suited you on these historic, tragic events, speaking of the Ustasha committing acts of genocide against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally expressed myself freely. But in the 1980s, there were threats of repressive measures by the regime, and I experienced many of these. Secondly, in 1990, Tudjman won in Croatia and he stated that he was continuing the traditions of that Ustasha regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen to the questions and answer them, if you can. Do you accept that returning people's memories to these events would serve the purpose of dividing society, making people feel more separate, creating, in a sense, a "them and us" society? Do you accept that's what doing this achieved?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. On the Serb side, no one drew attention to this in an organised way. First of all, the families of victims from World War II, as soon as the government changed, started organising themselves and started excavating the mass graves and burying their nearest and dearest, in real cemeteries, near churches and so on. This was not a manipulation of the victims. It was the first time people were free to bury the victims according to their moral, ethical, and religious norms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally on this general topic: Do you accept that the two types of events, taking people back to earlier suffering and where it happens, dividing people by creating a "them and us" culture, are two of the events which, when they coincide, can lead people all too easily to commit grave and sometimes genocidal crimes? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. It's not true. In this war, there were no genocidal crimes, in this last war. Although you here have forged information about Srebrenica and tried to prove genocide, that is false and it will not hold water, at least not in the court of history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I be clear about one thing: The mass graves, you say, were opened in the early 1990s. Were they located in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were mass graves in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look -- take that document back. It's an existing exhibit. It doesn't need to be dealt with further. Can we look now at a cover page from issue 9 of 1990s Velika Srbija magazine, your party's magazine. Perhaps we can display one and a second on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. 46b. If we could just put the map on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This has a headline and a passage at the bottom. The headline reads: "From Ohrid to the beaches of the Adriatic, everywhere are the guards of General Draza!" Perhaps you'd just explain that to us briefly.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that this is in verse. It rhymes. It is a folk song, two verses from a folk song. From Lake Ohrid to the beaches of the Adriatic, everywhere are the guards of General Draza. Do you want me to explain Serb folk poetry to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm really more interested in the bottom left-hand entry. But before we come to that: The map that we're looking at is what? Is this the map of Velika Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the map of Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this is a map that incorporates what others would say to be Bosnia and significantly large parts of what others would say to be Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, why others? I say that this map includes Bosnia. It doesn't, however, include Croatia. These are Serbian lands. And it is the Serbian people who live here. Orthodox Serbs, Muslim Serbs, and Catholic Serbs. I explained that to you on the first day, and this map confirms what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your definition that they themselves don't accept. The passage at the bottom reads whether from --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "Brother Serb, don't forget! These are Serbian lands!"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, what effect did you intend to have on those who might read this magazine in 1990, by announcing that land regarded by others as definitely in other territories, Bosnia and Croatia? What effect did you intend to have by publishing a magazine with this on its, I think, front page, or wherever?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have shown here was on the back. But a similar map was published in another issue of the magazine on the front page. So you're not far wrong. Secondly, I say here, quite clearly, or rather, we who edited the journal, said: "Brother Serb, don't forget!" Thirdly, you say something that's definitely Bosnia and Herzegovina and that's definitely Croatia. But you should know that in history nothing is definite. Not even that Great Britain of yours is definite. Who knows what history will bring with it. But this is a solemn statement: "Brother Serb, don't forget! These are Serb lands!" This is what we are leaving as a heritage to our children and grandchildren. These are Serbian lands, and one day they should all be Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1990, and you were publishing, being allowed to publish, material that would simply encourage people to go and fight, at the same time as you were saying things that would remind them of the terrible misfortunes of the Second World War. Do you realise how dangerous you were at the time, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not dangerous at all. I was representing a Serbian national value at that point in time, which many did not recognise but I was aware of. Secondly, the year 1990 was a year where one could already sense the breakup of Yugoslavia. Slovenian separatism was on the rise. Tudjman was already in power. We established this journal in July 1990, and Tudjman came to power in May 1990. It is two months after Tudjman's rise to power that we established the journal "Greater Serbia." And thirdly, in the 1980s, before Mr. Milosevic came to power, the atmosphere in Belgrade was already somewhat more liberal. Vladimir Dedijer published a huge book, a collection of documents on the Vatican and Jasenovac. Milan Bulajic published several volumes of books about the Ustasha genocide. And then Antun Miletic, who is a Croat --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this exhibit please be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, do you have the original of this volume?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we've got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To get a proper view of the map. It's a very inadequate photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll see if we've got a better version. I'll make an inquiry and I'll come back to it in a couple minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number, 902.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we've got an original, I'll ask that the original be produced, at least for the Court record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on a little now to one or two videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Vukovar, what was the justification for Serbs taking Vukovar? Just help us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Vukovar was a Serbian town, always. Secondly, just before the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? What was its population at the time that it was attacked, in percentage terms?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar was not attacked. Vukovar was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time it was liberated, what was its ethnic composition in percentage terms?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall - it's not 100 per cent reliable - neither the Serbs nor the Croats had an absolute majority. There was approximately an equal percentage of Serbs and Croats. And then there were some other nationalities. But neither the Serbs nor the Croats had more than 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these real Croats who spoke the Chakavian or the Kajkavian dialect or were they phoney Croats who spoke the Shtokavian dialect but somehow thought they were Croats? What were they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Phoney Croats, who spoke the Shtokavian dialect. And the centuries-long policies of the Catholic Church had deceived them into thinking they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The people who died and the people who were suffering in the course of being liberated were in fact, on your own reckoning, Serbs, but somehow they had to be punished or dealt with or killed, in some greater interest. They were actually Serbs. They didn't know it; they thought they were Croats. They were actually Serbs. So what is it that the Serbs are doing attacking other Serbs, on your understanding of history?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't the Serbs who were attacked. Croatian paramilitary units attacked the JNA barracks in Vukovar. That's how the conflict started. Secondly, in Vukovar, Croatian paramilitary units of Franjo Tudjman turned up and started maltreating the Serb Orthodox population before the conflict broke out. They attacked Serb Orthodox villages around Vukovar, and you should know that in World War II, Bobota, a huge Serbian village, and many villages in the surroundings, were made Catholic by force in World War II in order to turn them into alleged Croats as well. The Serbs there were upset by the rise of Franjo Tudjman to power. Their existence was threatened. The Croatian paramilitary units were the first to attack. They attacked the JNA barracks in Vukovar, and that's how the conflict broke out. So it was not the Serbs who attacked; it was the Croatian paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you go as far as to say that Tudjman also was a Serb who thought he was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Tudjman is German by origin, and that's a well-known fact. His very name means "foreigner," Tudjman, "foreign man." That's his last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd look at -- we've got a transcript for the next short clip, please. It's number 56, for the booth. If this could be distributed. This is on Sanction, I'm reminded to inform the technical booth. Shall we just play this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is the strongest Ustasha stronghold. When Vukovar falls, the Ustasha will have no chance. It is understood that someone who came here to fight voluntarily, he knows why he has come and what he is fighting for. You don't have to persuade him to go into battle. "We quickly gained this trust, and then the regime gave us a barrack in Bubanj Potok. They provided a whole barracks for SRS volunteers. And we gathered volunteers in Belgrade, here we would get uniforms for them, weapons for them, transport to the front, and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was only really concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Customary forgeries or falsifications on these BBC videotapes once again. Mr. Seselj never uttered the word "Serbia." Not once. And in the subtitles you saw the word "Serbia" repeated three times whereas Mr. Seselj didn't utter the word "Serbia" once in what he said. So I don't know how you can allow the use of forgeries of this kind from one day to the next. BBC's forgeries, falsifications are quite unbelievable. They're unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If that is so, we are grateful to you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will have in mind, since the difficulties with the passages that are on the film, we've been having fresh translations done, and I'm concerned with the first passage that the witness will have seen. No reference to the word "Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you said, Mr. Seselj, as we can see, a head of a group of armed men initially, was that, "This is the strongest Ustasha stronghold. When Vukovar falls, the Ustasha will have no chance. It's understood that someone who came here to fight voluntarily, he knows why he has come and what he is fighting for. You don't have to persuade him to go into battle." So help us, please: What were your men, Seselj's men who went to Vukovar, going there to do?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went to fight for the freedom of Vukovar and to rout the Ustasha formations which had taken control of Vukovar. And the Ustashas are Croatian fascists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember I asked you right at the beginning of the time when I was asking you questions how you were going to discriminate between Ustasha and non-Ustasha, between civilians and non-civilians? How in Vukovar were the civilians to be protected, those unfortunate civilians who thought themselves to be Croats?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the JNA protected all civilians; Orthodox Serbs, Catholics, and everybody else. Secondly, the Ustashas publicly and openly exposed themselves in Vukovar in what they called the National Guards Corps. So that was an Ustasha paramilitary formation belonging to Franjo Tudjman, completely illegally established. To the north of Vukovar, in Osijek, there was even Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a formation which existed which openly said of itself that it was Ustasha, and that was Glavas formation. They wore black uniforms, copied along the lines of the uniforms worn by the Ustashas during World War II. And the Serb people could differentiate between Ustashas and Croats very well. They never mixed the two up, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were your men going there knowing that they were expected to kill people who they found there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I constantly held speeches sending off the volunteers from Belgrade. I said that -- told them how Serb soldiers should behave. They should behave courageously and bravely on the battlefield and I told them how they should behave towards civilians, prisoners of war, the wounded from the opposite side and so on and so forth, their code of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... use that term "cleansing." Any operation to cleanse an area of one ethnic group inevitably brings the risk of violence and death, doesn't it, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does he agree that there was an operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, not at the moment. That's a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm coming to it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But any effort -- let's assume --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are intentionally -- do you wish me to answer, Mr. Nice, as far as the cleansing is concerned? You are intentionally falsifying facts by confusing two issues: Military cleansing, or mop-up, military mop-up of the terrain, which is a completely legitimate and legal military operation, and ethnic cleansing, which is absolutely prohibited pursuant to international laws. So you are confusing and mixing up the issues, consistently, not only in this case but in many other cases too. The mop-up operation is an operation to -- or rather, cleansing operations are to deal with pockets of resistance that remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go back, then, to clarifying --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume you are following the interpreters, and they're not shouting, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Clarifying the position. We're dealing here with ethnic cleansing and I'll ask the question again, in case you didn't understand it. Any exercise of ethnic cleansing comes with the inevitability of violence and death, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If ethnic cleansing existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what you mean by it existed. Ethnic cleansing happens, does it not, Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you want me to state my views about what ethnic cleansing brings with it, and then you would go on to interpret my answer as saying that there really was ethnic cleansing. That is a trick you can play on small children. You're not on a par with me, Mr. Nice. You can't pull tricks like that on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... which, as you've been told, is your function. If somebody, a military leader or --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Nice is asking this question of the witness highly improperly. In his first formulation, he said "cleansing the terrain from members or of members of other ethnic groups." That was the formulation. The transcript has left the screen in that portion, but he said "cleansing the terrain of other ethnic groups." So his question, to start with, was wrong and improper. Nobody has heard of terrain mop-up or cleansing of other ethnic groups or nationalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think there's any need to rephrase, in my respectful submission. The witness is declining to answer the question, but I'm going to ask it once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If a military commander, Mr. Seselj, or even somebody having command over military forces not counting himself as a military commander, instructs people to engage in ethnic cleansing, he knows, does he not, that violence and death will follow?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abstractly speaking, if we take it in the abstract, away from the facts, and reject the possibility that you are trying to abuse my answer, then yes, of course. If a military commander orders ethnic cleansing, he is conscious that that will lead to additional crimes. Anybody ordering ethnic cleansing. But you still have not, among the high-ranking Serb commanders, found a single one who ordered ethnic cleansing to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anybody sent in to Vukovar, for example, to drive the Croats back to the Karlobag-Virovitica line would be being instructed to do something that was bound to bring violence and death; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, nobody received instructions to push back or drive back the Croats from the Karlobag-Virovitica line, but to rout the Croatian paramilitary formations of Franjo Tudjman. Until the end of 1990, according to my information, the General Staff of the JNA was preparing a plan to completely rout Tudjman and to take control of Zagreb, to completely rout his paramilitary formations. Because the General Staff of the JNA wished the entire area of Croatia to remain within the composition of Yugoslavia. You don't like hearing this from me. It doesn't correspond with what you wish to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now look at an extract, 56A. Have we got extracts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you exhibiting the last document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. May I exhibit the last passage, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the number for that one, the last one, 56?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video clip, and together with the transcript, they will be 903.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to play you now a short extract, a broadcast publication. It was first seen in the opening of this case, a long time ago, and hasn't been produced since formally. There's some singing by Chetniks on this. We're going to have the words that they said underneath in English, and I'd like you, please, to listen, if you can - it's probably a song you know or singing which you recognise - and tell us if what we've got in English, which I'll read over to you, is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The regulars were celebrating in the streets that they had fought for and singing a tribal song against the Croats."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Try again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The regulars were celebrating in the streets that they had fought for and singing a tribal song against the Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that a song that speaks of "Slobo sending a salad, there will be plenty of meat, we will slaughter the Croats"? Is that what they were singing?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that is a song which was first sung by football supporters at the end of the 1980s at football stadiums. This song might have been sung somewhere here, but you ought to see who did the singing and what the motives for that were. The song was not an official song, and it was never sung by the members of the Serbian Radical Party. And of course, there are all sorts of songs, there were all sorts of songs sung by all sides in the previous war, the last war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did it contain the words that the Prosecutor has put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard better this next time, and yes, those are the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the "Slobo" to whom reference is made is whom?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask those singing the song. I never sung a song like that in my life, so I cannot interpret for you this pseudo-national songs which belong to the dregs of society, don't they? So the people who sang them can tell you. I never sang them. These are the dregs of the folk songs of society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you tell who we were looking at in the film?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You saw soldiers. We were looking at soldiers. Which soldiers, I don't know. I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably. But what needs to be done is to identify who those were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. You say that. Didn't you see the flag they were looking at? We might have to go back and have a look at it. Would you like to have a look at the flag? Just tell us. We needn't even --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the traditional Chetnik flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But one should bear in mind one fact here: After the breakdown of Communism, the pendulum that the communists had moved to one side for half a century by attacking the Chetniks as their ideological adversaries within the Serb people swung back to the other side. And in this war, we had the following fact: That practically all the Serb fighters were referred to as Chetniks, or other people considered them to be Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, this is the point, isn't it? I was going to come to this: These appear to be Serb Chetniks in the Serb Chetnik Party -- Movement, Serb Chetnik Movement. Remind us again: What was your connection to that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the Chetnik Movement did not appear from the 1st of August, 1991 anywhere as such on the fronts, on the front lines. When the Serb Chetnik Movement united, which was established in Serbia as a political party, with the bulk of the national Radical Party as members, it continued to work within the Serbian Radical Party, as a sub-organisation, which nurtured the freedom-loving traditions of the Serbian people. And in 1995, we disbanded the Serbian Chetnik Movement, giving the following explanation, and you can find that in one of my books, that explanation. We gave the explanation, and today all Serbian freedom lovers are considered to be Chetniks. And the Chetnik Movement is an all-Serb tradition and that no political party has the right to appropriate it. And here, you have no proof or evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These men described as the dregs of society would appear to be under the banner of the Serb Chetnik Movement at entry into Vukovar, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, this is not a flag of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and nowhere on it does it say the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Take a better look at that flag, the banner. This is one of the -- one possible Serb banners, but not the flag of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Secondly, you will see that all these soldiers, judging by their helmets, are JNA, which was not characteristic for the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. They avoided wearing these helmets because there was the five-pointed star, red five-pointed star on the helmets and they preferred to go bareheaded. So somebody started singing that song spontaneously. I did not say that these were the people of the dregs of society. It was the song that was generated and came into being with these low-level society people and it was sung first of all by football supporters during these football matches. And you can see that everybody here is wearing helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A lot of beards, there's a man in the middle with the kokarda hat. Doesn't this all look to you like Chetniks of your group, of which you were the leader? Doesn't it? Commander, I'm reminded.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I wasn't a commander. And secondly, I was, in a sense, the leader of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. I was president of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, if you consider that to be a leader. However, here we're dealing quite obviously with a particular unit. The banner is not the flag of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. I can send you an original to have a look and see what it looks like, and that's not this flag. This is partially the Chetnik flag but it just says "freedom or death" at the bottom, as far as I can read. So it doesn't say the Serbian Chetnik Movement. While the Serbian Chetnik Movement existed, it said on the flag "Serbian Chetnik Movement."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were, of course, the Vojvoda, weren't you? You've told us all about that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a Vojvoda, I am still a Vojvoda and will be a Vojvoda until the end of my life. I am very proud of having that title of a Serbian Vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I have that produced as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Is there a problem with the numbering of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think it's been exhibited. It was produced, I think -- it was screened in the opening, but it wasn't actually subsequently produced, so I think it hasn't been exhibited. So it needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's work on that basis. Please give it the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number will be 904.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll now look at another short extract, and I'll distribute the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we know where this footage was taken; what location, when, where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's said by the reporting journalist, Martin Bell, to be at Vukovar. That's what we know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did that journalist tell you that the singing of that song was intentionally sung for the filming? That's possible too. It wouldn't be the first time that this song was requested. Because I can see that you had some very successful cooperation with journalists. So that is highly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next extract, please -- next film, rather. And this is the journalist Baron van Lynden, from whom you've heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next tab, Your Honours, has the voice and may indeed have the image of Baron van Lynden, who has appeared as a witness here, and he then sets the scene for what is more important, which is what the soldier says. Perhaps we can play that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "van Lynden: ... reached the hospital of ... the blood still fresh, were clearly murdered. If the ruins of Vukovar symbolise anything at all, it must be the hatred that still exists between Serbs and Croats, that lay dormant during 45 years of peace, has now expressed itself in a mutual commitment to war, a commitment which does not appear to have been satisfied even after three months of fighting here."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go back to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't receiving the interpretation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My error. I didn't announce the tab for the interpreters. Number 57. So if they've found that, and if we can go back to the beginning. We should be able to provide interpretation for the witness, because I think Baron van Lynden speaks, I hope, at a comparatively moderate speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "van Lynden: ... who never reached the hospital, or who, the blood still fresh, were clearly murdered. If the ruins of Vukovar symbolise anything at all, it must be the hatred that still exists between the Serbs and Croats, that lay dormant during 45 years of peace, has now expressed itself in a mutual commitment to war, a commitment which does not appear to have been satisfied even after three months of fighting here. And amongst the horror, there is the surreal incongruity of celebration. Extremist Serb militiamen and women, posing triumphantly for an end-of-battle photograph, before returning to a morning feast of music and laughter, fuelled by alcohol. The motto on their flag is 'Freedom or Death,' and they vow they will fight on. "What, for you, do the Serbs need to take before the war is over? "The war will be over when we have our limits - Karlobag, Karlovac, Ogulin and Virovitica. All place where Serbian people live must be free, you know. We must clean up with the Croatians. "In the town centre other militiamen display an uncontrolled rejoicing, in a similar frame of mind."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, a couple of questions. First of all, the flag. What do you say about the flag? Whose flag was that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the flag of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. This is a flag that was handmade by individuals who do not know exactly what Serbian Chetnik heraldics looks like. It could have been inspired by the Chetnik Movement, but he is still an ignoramus in that area. Secondly, the statement has been requested by your journalist, quite obviously. I would have liked to have heard it in the Serbian language. Was it originally given in the English or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first bearded soldier we saw, the heavily bearded soldier who crossed himself, would he, from his appearance, appear to be one of Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean looking at the beard?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never wore a beard in my life. Or you mean because he's making the sign of the cross? Every Serb that is making the sign of a cross might be a Seselj man, or wears a beard must be a Seselj's man. That's not serious. This is the first time I see this man, so I can't say who he is or what he is. As to the person giving the statement to van Lynden, it is possible to identify that person. And instead of van Lynden, you should have brought him in to testify, to say whether that statement was commissioned by the journalist or whether he was inspired by my slogans or what he meant by what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, as, without a doubt, that person had to have given a statement in Serbian, we ought to hear what he says. We only had the translation, the interpretation from the English transcript, not the words of the witness, who allegedly is saying that in front of a television camera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you think -- are you questioning the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the person was speaking in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the soldier spoke in English. The soldier spoke in English, according to this video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we play it again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's hear that Serb Chetnik speaking in English, then. I'd really like to see someone like that and hear him, and I'm sure the viewers in Serbia will appreciate hearing a Serbian Chetnik speaking in English. Let's hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we play it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need the interpretation. Let me hear him in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Van Lynden: If the ruins of Vukovar symbolise anything at all, it must be the hatred that still exists between the Serbs and Croats, that lay dormant during 45 years of peace and has now expressed itself in a mutual commitment to war, a commitment which does not appear to have been satisfied even after three months of fighting here. And amongst the horror, there is the surreal incongruity of celebration. Extremist Serb militiaman and women, posing triumphantly for an end-of-battle photograph, before returning to a morning feast of music and laughter, fuelled by alcohol. The motto on their flag is 'Freedom or Death,' and they vow that they will fight on. "Unknown soldier: No, it's not finished. "Van Lynden: What, for you, do the Serbs need to take before the war is over? "Unknown soldier: War will be over when we have our limits - Karlobag, Karlovac, Ogulin, Virovitica. All place where Serbian people live must be free, you know. We must clean up with the Croatians. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "Van Lynden: In the town centre, other militiamen display an ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There you have it, Mr. Milosevic, your Serb Chetnik speaking English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I can see a Croatian flag that was unfolded at the end, and Mr. Seselj didn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the quality of the footage wasn't very good, but quite obviously he can't differentiate between a Croatian and Serbian flag. This whole video has been commissioned, the statement has been commissioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the flag that was unfolded at the end had the chequerboard emblem, Croatian chequerboard emblem on it. This is all quite a circus.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your person found a Croat to give him the kind of statement that he wanted to hear to ascribe to the Serbs as being people who were ethnically cleansing the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought they were just about burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About burning the flag, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now can I be allowed to ask the question to you, Mr. Seselj, please. You, I think, went to Vukovar after the events there, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Vukovar after the liberation of Vukovar, to celebrate the first anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You weren't there during the fighting, but you went there shortly --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there twice during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This soldier, who happens to speak in English, expresses the view that "War will be over when we have our limits - Karlobag, Karlovac, Ogulin, Virovitica." That sentiment, I suppose, would accord with your own desires, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. You're insinuating here. First you have to identify the soldier, and then let's see what he said and what his motives were. You know, this is as if you said he raped an unknown girl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question, very simply, was whether the view expressed by the soldier that the limits for the Serbs should be Karlobag, Karlovac, Ogulin, and Virovitica, whether that accords with your sentiment. I have heard you express something very close to that, if not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to say something very similar to that several times, and perhaps even that itself. But I am never going to confirm for you that the opinion of this unknown soldier matches mine. Because I am interested in the motives for the statement he made. In the first part of his statement, there is a similarity with the ideology of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a different issue. But it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just would like to be clear about one thing. It's not related to this passage, it's much earlier in your evidence, when there was reference to the early 1990s and the mass graves of Serbs being opened at that stage. And just slightly earlier in your evidence, you refuted the suggestion that the killings, the genocide during the Second World War had been caused by Ustashas. Now, did I catch that correctly? You refuted that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the Second World War, the Ustashas, the Croatian Ustashas, carried out a genocide against the Serb people. You have the testimony of Hitler's envoy in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies. I thought you had denied that, in fact, in your answer, but you now clarify that that was the position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Perhaps you got the wrong interpretation. I said that at this particular war, now, there was no genocide. Because I know the definition of genocide very well, from the international convention. This war that was waged now, in the 1990s, and there was no genocide then. There were different war crimes, but the crime of genocide was not committed. I was clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think I know what Judge Bonomy is referring to, and I'll search it in the break. Let's adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last question I wanted to ask you about the document we were looking at before the break - it's not shown on the overhead projector at the moment, but I can read it out to you - is this: A soldier in Vukovar at the time of the incident at Vukovar, the events at Vukovar, saying that all places where Serbian people must be free and saying, in English: "We must clean up with the Croatians" sounds to be a soldier who understands his mission to be to move Croats to the Karlobag-Virovitica line, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I think there's a problem involved here in the translation. And I need an interpretation of this. What it says here in the original: "[In English]... clean up with the Croatians." [Interpretation] I, who does not speak English, only a bit and only from time to time, I interpret this as meaning "we have to clear things up with the Croats." And what the interpreter interpreted for me here was: "We have to cleanse the Croats." Am I right? "We must clean up with the Croatians." I mean, you speak English better than I do, does that mean to settle accounts with Croats or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that what should be there is: "We must clear up things with the Croatians"? Because in that event, I think we should hear it again. It was in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English text right in front of me. It says: [In English] "Clean up with the Croatians." [Interpretation] And the interpreter gave me a different interpretation, "We have to cleanse the Croats."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point is well made, I think, but it's a matter for the Court to interpret in the light of the context in which it's said. And we could debate this forever. I take note of the comment Mr. Seselj makes, which has some foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I entirely agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Seselj, you see, if we look at the previous sentence, or the two previous sentences, a soldier identifying Karlobag-Virovitica borders and saying, "All places where Serbs live must be free, you know," sounds like a soldier whose mission it is to move the Croats back beyond that border. Do you not agree?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This doesn't sound like a soldier to me. This is an unknown soldier. Something like the tomb of the unknown soldier. I don't know whether he's a soldier, I don't know what his name is or why he made such a statement or for what purposes or what his motives are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the previous transcript but one, where you were speaking and you said: "It is understood that someone who comes here to fight voluntarily, he knows why he has come and what he is fighting for." And I gave you a chance to answer that, and my suggestion to you is that your soldiers in Vukovar knew that they were fighting for the cause that would push Croats, if successful, beyond that line, the Karlobag-Virovitica line. That's my suggestion to you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Croats, as a people, or rather, those who, though being Serb Catholics, declared themselves to be Croats, it's not them I was talking about. I was talking about Croatian paramilitaries. As for our line, Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica, it means that all Serb Catholics which were used to create Croats artificially over 100 years, they should live together with Serb Orthodox, Serb Muslims and all others. That is the core of my statements. I'm not going to refute a single statement of mine. But linking up my statements to statements made by an unknown soldier, then I'm not even going to -- I cannot confirm that for you, because it's impossible, that that unknown soldier is saying what I'm saying. Even if he repeats my words verbatim, I'm not going to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we exhibit, please, this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 905.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you now, please, to view with us a short patch from an interview in August 1991. The transcript is coming.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 68. And this comes from TV Benkovac. I beg your pardon. This comes from RHT Croatian TV, I think. Let's play it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Are your volunteers a legitimate army or do they fall within the category of paramilitary units? "We are not establishing any kind of paramilitary formations here in this narrowed-down Serbia. We are only gathering volunteers here and sending them where they are needed, to Serbian Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem and Serbian Krajina. And these volunteers place themselves under the command of local Serbian commanders living there and carry out orders regarding their activity on the battlefield. Therefore, we are not engaged in establishing any paramilitary formations and we are opposed to any kind of paramilitary formations. "Are you commander of all those forces? "Yes, I'm the commander of all the volunteers over there. "And can you control the situation? "Yes. I can. So far, I have always exercised control over the situation and all our volunteers are well disciplined. We do not have any problems with them. We prohibit the use of alcohol and only those who are capable of fighting, who are disciplined, who execute all tasks given to them, and who act valiantly towards the enemy. You will not be able to find any Croat who will complain about maltreatment, unless he had a weapon in his hand and was attacking Serbian villages. In particular, you would not be able to find a Croat woman or child who have been mistreated by the Serbs ... which is not the case with the Croats. The Croats are once again perpetrating awful crimes against the Serb civilian population."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you'll see that we set the particular passage in which we're interested in a broader context of your denying any intent to be involved with or to form paramilitary organisations and your assertion of the discipline of those in your volunteer forces. What I'm interested to know is this: You were asked the very simple question: "Are you the commander of those forces?" And you replied: "Yes, I am the commander of the volunteer forces over there." Can you explain that to us, in light of your evidence to the Court?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Of course I can, Mr. Nice, with great pleasure. You see that I give this statement in short sleeves, in a shirt. So it is summertime. You should have the date of the interview. Obviously you haven't got it. The interview was made right after the battle --
