utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: August --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this. You asked for an explanation. Please. This was made before the JNA was involved in armed conflicts. Perhaps it was aired only in August, but it had to be filmed by July, at the latest. Because after the battle in Borovo Selo, we sent several groups of volunteers to Borovo Selo and to the other villages, expecting Croat attacks and retaliation for the defeat they suffered in Borovo Selo. I state quite clearly here that I'm responsible for these volunteers. Perhaps "command" would be too strong a word. I cannot command them from Belgrade. But I explain here under whose command they are. I clearly state, though, that I bear responsibility for them and their behaviour. That would be the right way of putting it. But that was before the JNA was involved in the conflicts. As soon as the JNA got involved in the conflicts, our volunteers only went into the JNA. So that had to be filmed by the end of July, at the latest. And I'm not denying at all that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can that be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look, then, briefly, at -- this again is a television interview.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have a reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 66. Apologies. Just play that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Wait a second! On those army helmets we ... you know what, guys. I'm used to everybody being silent while I am talking. Perhaps you still haven't developed this habit, but I have. We painted two-headed Serbian white eagles on the helmets, and the army officer, captain, major, commands our people. And by coordinated action, Kameni, our chief commander in Vukovar, plans the action in cooperation with the army major in the evening, and they carry it out the following day. Because of soldiers deserting from their units, the army did not have enough manpower to go from house to house and take it over, so our people did that. Army strikes with tanks, mortars, Howitzers, and our people go from house to house and conquer it. Don't you tell me now that this is a communist army. They took off the five-pointed star insignias and they did not ask us to take our cockades off."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is later in 1991, it appears September. Painting two-headed Serbian white eagles on your helmets. Why did your group do that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is not September. It can be November 1991, and obviously it's in Benkovac. It's the same footage that you showed yesterday, but it's a different part. This is my verbal duel with Captain Dragan. I think it's part of the same clip. So that's November 1991. First of all, you did not show it in its entirety. I am trying to persuade the soldiers here to wear helmets for the sake of their own protection. And these helmets that have five-pointed red stars on them should be covered by a two-headed white eagle, because that is the Serbian national symbol and has been so for over 1.000 years. But if a Serb puts a two-headed white eagle on his helmet, that does not mean that he belongs to the paramilitaries of the White Eagles, lest there be any misunderstanding. The white eagle is now the coat of arms of Serbia. Serbia had a communist coat of arms until only a few years ago and throughout 1991 we waged a campaign to get the communist red five-pointed star off the army insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there not a suitable Yugoslav, rather than Serbian, symbol that could have been put on the helmets of the Yugoslav National Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two-headed white eagle was a Yugoslav symbol, between the two World Wars, of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood you. You did say clearly already that it was a Serbian symbol. That was why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, in order to be very precise about this: For over 1.000 years, a two-headed white eagle has been the symbol of Serbia. In the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, in addition to the cross, the coat of arms received, in addition to the Serbian white eagle, the Croatian coat of arms and the Slovenian coat of arms. So all of it put together was the coat of arms of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. When Yugoslavia was established after the Second World War, the white eagle was re-established. However, in 1991, we could not reach agreement, so we offered a compromise; to have insignia in the colours of the Yugoslav flag and to have that put on the helmets and caps of the army. However, that was not possible until Veljko Kadijevic was overthrown. He wanted a red star at all costs. The big problem was that not only our volunteers but many other soldiers did not want to wear helmets, so there were far more casualties than would have been the case otherwise, especially in the rocky terrain of Benkovac, because bullets would ricochet and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the White Eagles paramilitary groups did wear helmets with white eagles on them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they didn't wear helmets. They were just called the White Eagles. That was their name, like the Yellow Wasps. The Yellow Wasps did not have insignia of wasps or wasps' nests, they were simply called The Wasps, The Yellow Wasps. Maybe you'd be interested in this, Mr. Nice, if I may tell you about this. Maybe you will find it interesting. Are you interested?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... topic, please. We see here in what you said that you speak of your commander in Vukovar, Kameni, he was a man with whom you were quite close, wasn't he? Did he become your bodyguard at one stage?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was never my bodyguard. But he is a prominent commander from Vukovar. He became a member of the Serb Radical Party, and in the Serb Radical Party, I have the highest esteem for him and I consider him to be a personal friend. He was never my bodyguard. Immediately after the war, he had two apoplexies and I think that his health is rather precarious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was the commander at the time, and you make it clear that he had regular contact with the army majors and carried out the operations on a daily basis, following discussions with the army major in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a story I'm telling in Benkovac, and it's not very precise. The point of the story is not to describe the situation in Vukovar, but to persuade people to wear helmets. Kameni was the commander of the Leva Supoderica Territorial Defence unit in Vukovar. When the Guards Brigade, the detachment, became part of that brigade, on the orders of the commander of the Guards Brigade, the fighters of the Serb Radical Party were sent to that detachment under the command of Kameni. And these are the facts as they stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to try and get a feel for your position at the time. Here you are in November 1991 speaking for all the world, isn't it, as though you have a measure of command over your men? Do you not accept that that's the way it sounds, if you just look at that interview?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can sound that way, but that interview is from July 1991, at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This interview, the one we've been looking at, you told us is in November, in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And where does it say here that I'm the commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The way you demand silence, the way you tell people what to do. Doesn't it look as though you have some command over your men? I'm just asking you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to what I was doing, persuading people to wear helmets, there was yet another problem. These volunteers who were there complained about some JNA officers. And I was convincing them that they have to be highly disciplined. And then they said that officer is a communist and behaves in such-and-such a way. Then I was trying to convince them that they had to be disciplined. So this is political activity on my part. And of course I'm used to having everyone keep silent while I talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you look, please, at the following document. It's an existing exhibit, Exhibit 458, tab 20. And it's, for the interpreters, it's tab 60. If you'd like to look at the original of this, please. Dated now the 9th of December, 1991, and it's from the Territorial Defence municipal staff in Vukovar, and it's a request that the Chetnik -- English version on the overhead projector, please, Mr. Nort -- the Chetnik commander of Vukovar, Captain Katic -- we'll get you another English version rather -- that's good. Katic, from Zemun, hereby asks the chief of the war staff, Ljubisa Petkovic, and his deputy, Zoran Rankic, from Belgrade, to propose the following warriors for promotion. Then there's a list: Milan Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Lancuzanin, Predrag Milojevic, Milovan Tomic, and so on. "Thank you in advance." And we see that those people who are requested for promotion come from the Leva Supoderica group, and so on.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that's not correct. There are only three men here from Leva Supoderica: Milan Lancuzanin, Predrag Milojevic, and Predrag Dragojevic. Secondly, who knows what this piece of paper means? Was this really signed by Slobodan Katic? Slobodan Katic was the deputy of Milan Lancuzanin Kameni, as far as I can remember. He is now proposing promotions. What did he mean by that? He's the one who has to be asked about this. As for Milan Lancuzanin Kameni, I proclaimed him a Serb Chetnik Vojvoda in 1993. That is the rank of a Serb Vojvoda, a Serb Chetnik Vojvoda. He was a captain first class in the army. Now, whether this is an original document or not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ljubisa Petkovic and Zoran Rankic, are chief of the war staff, but that's the war staff of what? Just help us, please. It's the war staff of your party, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, the war staff of the Serb Radical Party, where Ljubisa Petkovic was chief, he was vice-president of the party. But he's not being asked to promote anyone, because he cannot promote anyone. He is being asked to ask someone for these promotions. Who could that be? Somebody in the General Staff, whatever. Because all of these people were officers; reserve officers, active-duty-officers, I cannot say for sure. So they are asking the chief of the war staff to propose the following people for promotion. You really have to ask the people who wrote this to explain it. This is the first time in my life that I see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But it shows, doesn't it, you see, an integrated connection between your party, the war staff of your party, and members of the Leva Supoderica group.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you that Milan Lancuzanin Kameni joined the Serb Radical Party during the fighting for Vukovar. The Serb Radical Party has not denounced him, or never will. It's not only members of Leva Supoderica who are mentioned here. There is the chief of security of Vukovar, one is the commander of the Territorial Defence, one is the chief of the Territorial Defence, one is the commander of the Petrova Gora detachment, and then again some chief of security, and so on. Of these eight men, only three are from the Leva Supoderica detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These men who held commanding or responsible positions, did they serve for longer periods than the brief periods you indicated that the volunteers generally served for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were not volunteers from Serbia at all. These are local people from Vukovar. As far as I know, not a single one of them, except for Slobodan Katic, who allegedly signed this -- Slobodan Katic is from Belgrade. All the rest are from Vukovar, as far as I know. Some of the names here aren't familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Petkovic was the vice-president of the Serb Radical Party and the chief of its war staff. And he was our party's direct link to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're not suggesting that these weren't volunteers from the Serb Radical Party, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who says they were? These are warriors. That's what it says here. Not a single one is said to be a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what basis would there be for the chief of the war staff of the Serb Radical Party to make a proposal that they should be promoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, the text was evidently written by an uneducated man, somebody with perhaps only primary or secondary school. That's evident from the way it's composed. Secondly, whoever wrote this knew that Ljubisa Petkovic had a direct link with the General Staff and assumed that he had the authority to propose promotions, if we are speaking of military ranks, because if this was a promotion to the rank of Chetnik Vojvoda, I assume it would say so here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milosevic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the second is an original text. In the English translation, it says "The Chetnik commander of Vukovar." In the Serb original, it doesn't say "The Chetnik commander of Vukovar." It would say that. It says, however,"The Chetnik commander, the captain for Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you repeat your first point, because we didn't hear it because of no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This first sheet of paper is supposed to be a translation into English, and it says: "The Chetnik commander of Vukovar," which would be [B/C/S spoken] in Serbian. In the Serbian text, however, it says: "The Chetnik commander, the captain for Vukovar." That's something completely different. There's no mention of the fact that he's some sort of Chetnik commander of Vukovar. These are two different things. This is a completely wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I note the point. I think the matter is extremely minor, and it really doesn't bear on the question which I'm trying to get an answer to, which is that this clearly refers to the chief of the war staff, who the witness accepts is the chief of the war staff of the Serb Radical Party, making a proposal, or inviting, or being asked to propose warriors for promotion. Now, that all makes sense. He might actually be being asked to propose to the JNA that these warriors should be promoted. I see that. But what I'd like to know is whether they are volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, and that seems to be denied. So we can now move on, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's not being denied. It's a fact, as far as I know, that not a single one of these men was a volunteer of the Serb Radical Party except for Slobodan Katic himself, who allegedly signed this, if he did. He was a volunteer of the Serb Radical Party. He came to Vukovar from Belgrade to fight. All the rest are local men from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are denying that the eight men mentioned there are Serb Radical volunteers, so I have that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me return to the point --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to return to the point made by Mr. Milosevic to check whether the word "captain" has been omitted. Can the interpreters help us? Mr. Milosevic said that it should read: "The Chetnik commander, captain of Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the original text in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can it be laid on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it says "Chetnik commander captain for Vukovar, Slobodan Katic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question that I want your assistance with, Mr. Seselj: What, in December 1991, is such a person doing seeking authority from the chief of your party's war staff? Or not authority - support of this --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say support. He's looking for support. He's asking him to propose these people for promotion. You're asking me to explain a letter written by somebody else here. I can only interpret what the text says here. I'm seeing it for the first time. It says that he is requesting promotion for the following warriors. He doesn't even refer to them as volunteers. But Mr. Nice, I know for a fact that you have interviewed some of these people. You have their statements. The one whom you interviewed least --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at another document, please, which is tab 62, and the existing Exhibit 643, tab 7, be laid on the overhead projector. If you'd like to take the original. This comes shortly before the last document, I think, just at the end of November. And from OGU command, Negoslavci village, it regulates the issue of re-subordination and a return to home units. And it says: "Further to the newly arisen situation and the order of the 1st Military District, I order withdrawal of the Leva Supoderica volunteers, dispatch of the Kragujevac Sumadinac detachment," and various other troop movements. Then if we turn over in the English, and I think you go to the bottom of the page, you'll see it's signed by Colonel Mile Mrksic and it's copied, amongst other things, to the commander of the Seseljevci volunteers.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not a good translation, Mr. Nice. It doesn't say "withdraw," but "pull out," and "send into the composition of." So this is a redeployment, not a withdrawal. I have heard the interpretation that they are being withdrawn, but they are being pulled out and sent to another brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question that I'm asking you. It's addressed to the commander of the Seseljevci volunteers detachment. Now, if they weren't functioning as a separate body, who was this being addressed to, in fact?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see in point one it says the volunteer detachment, Leva Supoderica. That was its official name. Popularly, this detachment was referred to as Seselj's men, and when it says here "copied and delivered to the commander of the 'Seseljevci'" in quotation marks, it's actually the volunteer detachment called the Leva Supoderica that is being referred to. That was its official name. Unofficially, people called that detachment the Seseljevci because the majority of the men were volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. But this goes to confirm that it was under the command of the commander of the 1st Guards Brigade, because it was signed by Colonel Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were the Leva Supoderica entirely composed of Seseljevci or were there other troops in that detachment?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also local men from Vukovar, including the commander, Kameni. But most of them were Seseljevci. Well, I'll tell you how I interpret this document which I'm seeing for the first time. The commander of the Guards Brigade, who was also the commander of the south operative group, is withdrawing from Vukovar. The Guards Brigade in late 1991 withdrew from Vukovar, and he's issuing an order for the Leva Supoderica detachment to be pulled out of the 1st Guards Brigade and sent into the composition of the Infantry Motorised Brigade. It could be of the 12th Corps, I don't know what "12K" means. But this looks like an Infantry Motorised Brigade. So it is being pulled out of the 1st Guards Brigade and sent to be part of another unit. The Kragujevac detachment, popularly called the Sumadinac, was a detachment of the JNA that had arrived from Kragujevac, composed of permanent soldiers and reservists, and it is being sent into the first -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we move on to something different. In fact, we're going to move back just a year in time, or a year and a little bit in time before we move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd look at this, please, an extract from one of your books. This is from -- I'm sorry. It's tab number 74, and it, in a sense, brings us to Bosnia, because we're across the river from Zvornik, this was delivered at Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've given me something else, something that refers to Kosovo, from the book "The Serbian Chetnik Movement," my speech made in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mali Zvornik is not in Bosnia, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Across the river. I've already said that. Now can we just concentrate on what you said in 1990. You'll see it marked on page 65 of the original text. Perhaps, to avoid any translation problem, you'd be good enough to read out what you say in March 1990 about Kosovo and Metohija -- August 1990.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I have to tell you that Mali Zvornik is not across the River Drina. It's on this side of the Drina and it's an integral part of Serbia. You have to distinguish between Mali Zvornik and Zvornik. These have always been two separate municipalities, separated by the River Drina. I said in that speech: "Kosovo and Metohija are holy Serbian land. The Serbian people have fought wars a number of times in its history for Kosovo and Metohija, shed rivers of blood and a sea of human lives, and we, today's Serbians, will know how to appreciate this and we will shed new rivers of blood if need be, but Kosovo and Metohija will remain Serbian land." That's what I said, and I abide by this today, I will advocate this until the rest of my life and as long as there is a single Serb alive, the Serb people will not give up having Kosovo and Metohija as an integral part of Serbia. What I'm saying is that every Serb is prepared to die for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've had your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And although we're not going to produce the book, in fairness to you, there's been a consistency of approach, because right back in 1982, you were publishing in a book called "Self-reflection on a System and the Necessity for Change," you were publishing things about the forced evacuation of Albanians from territory that they occupied, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. This is a paper of mine in which I advocate solving the problem of Kosovo and Metohija. But this is from the 1980s. This is my scholarly work, later published in the book "Democracy and Dogma." And what I advocate is to have the conditions created for 200.000 Albanians to move to Croatia, 100.000 to Serbia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, to Slovenia, interpreter's correction. Could the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you are getting carried away. You're speaking too fast. The interpreters are asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Enough for the early 1980s.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a good thing for Mr. Nice to show this excerpt from my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we have time and if I choose to, we may. But I'm just trying to say that you had a consistent position. I want you to focus now on what you tell us would be the effect in 1990 of saying anywhere in the former Yugoslavia that "We will shed new rivers of blood, if need be." What was the likely effect of that sort of rhetoric on your Serb audience, please?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, for 50 years in Yugoslavia, it was said "We will shed rivers of blood for every foot of Yugoslav territory." That was the standard vocabulary in political life. "For every foot of territory, if need be, we will shed a river of blood." Secondly, every country in the world is prepared to defend every last piece of its territory by all means. This is a freedom-loving phrase spoken here, which is standard, and has been in the national tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you genuinely and sincerely asserting to this Court that to promise the listeners or the readers rivers of blood as a result of the pursuit of their political ambition is a standard, freedom-loving phrase? Really?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially with reference to Kosovo and Metohija. And I'm telling you, the vast majority of the Serbian people holds this position today. You will never wrest Kosovo and Metohija away from us. We will never be reconciled to this. We are ready to sacrifice ourselves again for Kosovo and Metohija as a nation, as we have done for centuries. This is simply holy land. Kosovo and Metohija is worth more than our continued existence as a people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why don't you put to him directly that it's the kind of language that would incite people to violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to ask one intervening question, with Your Honour's leave, and it's this:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whose blood should the reader infer would create the new rivers? Kosovar Albanians, Serbs, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice is saying that Mr. Seselj promised rivers of blood to his audience. That doesn't follow from this quotation. He did not promise rivers of blood to anyone. He used the expression "promising" his audience rivers of blood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may be a question of language, but I don't see anything unfair in the way the question was put, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, can you answer my question? Whose blood would make these new rivers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, it was always Serbian blood that was shed, first of all, and then the blood of Serbian foes, the foes of Serbia, who tried to wrest Kosovo and Metohija away from us. Kosovo and Metohija are part of Serbia. And that is my threat to all future enemies, whether British, American, whoever turns up to take away Kosovo and Metohija from us. We will not give it up, regardless of our sacrifices. And in the Kosovo myth, in the Kosovo tradition, it's always Serbian blood that is referred to, first and foremost. There is a flower growing, a red peony, in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is 1990, the development of events and the involvement of the international community couldn't be known. Of course the Serbs had lost in Kosovo before, as we all know. But when you say something like this in 1990 to a Serb audience, you're inciting your Serb audience to think of killing other people, aren't you? Obvious.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are falsifying this. This is not evident. I am inciting the Serbian people, if necessary, if somebody tries to wrest Kosovo and Metohija away from us, to sacrifice ourselves as a nation and to defend it, at all costs. Kosovo and Metohija is the very meaning of the existence of the Serbian people, and this battle is obviously not finished yet. If our generation does not finish it, it will be left for our sons, for our grandsons. But Kosovo and Metohija must remain in Serb hands, regardless of the victims that have to fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can this be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 908.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd like now, please, to look at another passage of yours. And we are coming to tab 74a, for the interpreters. We are still in 1991, although the topic is still Kosovar Albanians. This is from the book "Serbian Chetnik Movement," Programme Declaration of the Serbian Radical Party. Incidentally, before I move on, and I'm very grateful to Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff for her recollection: The things that we looked at in the last exhibit, about rivers of blood and so on, did you say anything critical of Mrs. Plavsic for saying such things in your evidence here? We'll find it, if necessary, but do you recall saying something critical of Mrs. Plavsic for saying such things?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Biljana Plavsic said was absolutely different from what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was part of what she said similar to what you said?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may look it up. We'll come back to it if we find it. But now let's look at this document, the Serbian Chetnik Movement. If you would go, please, to page 275 in the text in the language you understand. We'll look at page 12 in the English. And it's paragraph part 25. To avoid problems with interpretation or translation, would you please read the first six paragraphs of part 25 to us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the programme declaration of the Serb Radical Party. I have to say that first. It's the manifesto from 1991. In point 25, it says, inter alia -- I'm reading only what you marked, but I can read it all. I won't mind reading it all, if you want: "The stifling by all means of the Albanian separatist revolt in Kosovo and Metohija. In order to prevent a repeat of this revolt, we call for the urgent implementation of the following measures: "The efficient prevention of establishment of any form of Kosovo and Metohija political territorial autonomy. "To expel immediately all 360.000 Albanian immigrants and their offspring. "To prevent all state financial subsidies to the Albanian national minority, and all funds earmarked earlier for that purpose should be redirected solely to the financing of the return of Serbs to Kosovo and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Metohija. "A state of war should be proclaimed in Kosovo and Metohija, all political activity should be suspended, and martial law should be introduced to last at least ten years. "All organs of civilian authority and institutions there which are financed from the state budget and operate in Albanian, like the university, Academy of Arts and Sciences, and media and publishing houses should be dissolved immediately. "All factories and other production plants which are uneconomic because of the systematic sabotage of Siptar employees should be closed down immediately and mothballed." Do you want me to go on reading? I can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will be satisfactory for the time being, thank you. If asked, how, did you explain, were the 360.000 Albanian immigrants, as you describe them, to be expelled? What was the mechanics you were going to use?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for them to return to their country, Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the mechanics you were going to use? You must have thought about it, Mr. Seselj. You were allowed to publish this sort of thing. What mechanics were you going to use to get 360.000 people to move to Albania? Negotiation? Financial persuasion? Or force?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these immigrants from Albania were in Serbia and in Yugoslavia illegally, and they would all have been expelled in the same way that Western European countries expel illegal asylum-seekers; some by plane, some by bus, and so on. All those who are on our territory illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You understand the position: These are the people who you say had populated Kosovo and Metohija since the Second World War, so it included people who lived there for 40 years or thereabouts, and their children who lived there all their lives. And what were you going to do, give them court hearings and move them into detention centres while their claims for asylum or whatever else it might have been were dealt with, or were you just going to kick them out? Which?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is a programme declaration of the Serbian Radical Party. What the Serbian Radical Party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please answer the question. You've just been asked specifically how you would do it. Can you not turn to that very quickly and let's move, make some progress.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the same way, in the same way that Germany or France or England is expelling illegal immigrants, in that same way. The fact that their children were born in Serbia does not give them automatic right to Serb citizenship. They systematically came to populate Serbia. They acted from separatist positions, and that is the context. It is them who persecuted the Serbs over there and forced them to emigrate and leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I, as a judge sitting here, do not know how any of the three countries you have named deal with the removal of immigrants. I don't know that. I'm not able to compare it with what you are intending. So please tell me what your plan was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our plan was that anybody who did not have Serbian citizenship had to leave the territory of Serbia, in Kosovo and Metohija, when it came to Albanian immigrants. Now, we're not here -- we did not develop technology here, the ways and the means, the technical means, and the local authorities would do that, or the authorities would do that once they came into power. But anybody without our citizenship would have to leave. Some people would leave by buses, planes, cars, ships, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, before I come to put to you what I suggest is the truth about all this, Mr. Seselj, just let's remind the Court of what you told us and indeed what one of the journalists you're always attacking told us, Mr. Anastasijevic. This was at a time -- 1990, was a time when you were still in favour with the accused and you were allowed more access to state-run media than at other times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How far I was in favour with Mr. Milosevic in the 1990s is that his authorities put me in prison three times in 1990. That's what favour I enjoyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I just want to emphasise it. The publication of this programme of your party is at a time when you were still in favour with him and were given plenty of access to the media. So that what you set out here in your party programme is likely to have been reflected on interviews and speeches on the television. Do you follow me? Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what kind of favour are you talking about? I was never in anybody's favour, or Mr. Milosevic's favour. On the 23rd of February, in Kragujevac, we proclaimed the Serb Radical Party, and immediately after that, we compiled this programme declaration. And in the preamble, you can see that we did that on the basis of the programme and statute that was adopted in Kragujevac on the 23rd of February. What has that to do with Mr. Milosevic at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... answer the question. I'm going to suggest to you that your intention with these 360.000 Albanian immigrants, as you describe them, and their offspring, who had, many of them, spent their entire lives in Kosovo and Metohija, was simply to kick them out. By force. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In a legal way. Force based on law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where do we see the detail of that? Have you set out anywhere in your books or your programme the carefully regulated, internationally acceptable programme of court hearings, appeal hearings, and so on, to which these people would be entitled, and their children?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was implied, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the frameworks of a society governed by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we exhibit this document and then look at another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, which is tab 75, for the interpreters. It's another extract from Ustasha Phantasmagorias. And if you'd be good enough, please, to go to page 73, I think, in the original text, and if the Court would be good enough to go to page 13, at the foot. And perhaps Mr. Nort would lay the English text on the overhead projector, and we'll read just a little bit more of the areas marked, sidelined for particular reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was an election campaign speech, you see, the kind that would be carried on TV, radio, newspapers. And picking it up at the full paragraph, it says: "You have heard the basic aspects of our national programme. You are probably interested in knowing what kind of programme we are advocating in relation to the definite stifling of the Siptar separatist rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija. The Siptars are behaving to our benefit. They vastly refused to be registered in the most recent population census. You know that a population census is an obligation stemming from relevant United Nations documents, and all countries are obliged to conduct a population census once every ten years." Would you like to read to us, to avoid any problems with translation, the next sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Siptars have made our job easier. Those who boycotted the census are not our citizens and they do not have any reason to stay in our country. Simply, we shall surround them using the army and push them back across the border, to Albania. There will be a lot of noise in the West. They will make a lot of noise for a month or two, and eventually they will forget."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So as between what you said in your election speech, of course it was to the electorate, what you told the Judges a few minutes ago about what was the implied legal system you were going to employ, which is the truth? Because they can't both be.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, a moment ago, you had an official document of the Serbian Radical Party, and it contained what it contained. Now you have my individual speech, which isn't completely in keeping with the document of the Serbian Radical Party, for which the Serbian Radical Party could have punished me, but it did not. And I really did utter this, and there's no doubt about that. Now, you must differentiate between those two things, between an official document of the Serbian Party and what I said on one particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... lots of times, Mr. Seselj. This is one we've got recorded in your book, and in your book you don't say, "I'm very sorry I said this."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you? You don't say you're sorry you promised the Kosovar Albanians that you would push them out by military force, do you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the present day, I'm not sorry for having said this in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So despite what you said to this Court about five minutes ago or less, your actual intention in 1990, 1991 was that the Siptars, as you describe them, should be surrounded by the military and pushed out of the country in which they and their children have been living, many of them for all of their lives, and you did that because -- or you said that because you thought the West would make a bit of noise and then forget.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're falsifying matters again. A moment ago we had an official document of the Serbian Radical Party. If you have an official document of the Serbian Radical Party, then it is the official party policy, whereas this is my own statement. My statement is much sharper than the official policy of the party. All you can say is that. That's the only conclusion you can draw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I, unlike Mr. Nice, don't see any inconsistency between the two. Is there an inconsistency?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Insofar as I thought that he had said in answer that the proper inference from the document was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But the contents. There's no inconsistency between the contents of the document and what you actually said. One is the policy and the other is how you're going to implement it

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are inconsistencies, because the Serbian Radical Party never officially said anything of this kind. But I did personally. However, Mr. Nice has made an oversight here. We are dealing with disloyal Albanians who refused to go to the population census and be recorded by the census. So you know what happens there. You know what it means to boycott a population census. It means so you can have the falsifications and forgeries from the previous census in '81 and have a wrong impression of how many Albanians there are in Kosovo and so that Albanian immigrants can falsely be considered to be citizens of Serbia. So a distinction is made here between those who responded and did their civic duty by responding to the census and the others who boycotted it. That this statement is too sharp, it is, but it was uttered from my lips, and you won't find it in the document of the Serbian Radical Party. There we have it. I assume that's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say "too sharp," but either your intention was to move them out by military force or it wasn't. And all we want to know -- at least, all I want you to help the Court with, is whether your intention was that they should be moved out by military force.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I state a position rhetorically, and I won't go back on that. But I can't confirm that that's the actual way that I would throw them out, because I was a little angry when I delivered this speech. There's a little anger due to the conduct of the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija towards the Serbs living over there. Now, what you want to do now, in a much calmer atmosphere, for me to repeat that word by word. No, I'm not going to do it. I am saying that I said this, it was a propaganda speech, motivated by some specific thing that was happening, event that was happening during that time, during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we take it -- I was going to turn to Bosnia, but I'm just going to stick with Kosovo for a little bit, for one reason, in light of the time. There's something I want you to help us with. May we take it that your attitude to Kosovar Albanians starting as it did in the early 1980s, being expressed in your party's programme, and indeed in this speech in the early 1990s, can we take it that your attitude remained the same right through the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is improper. Mr. Nice is asking the witness about the position towards -- the attitude towards Kosovar Albanians, whereas here we're quoting not the attitude towards Kosovar Albanians but illegal immigrants, which is quite a different matters. Kosovar Albanians are one thing, non-Kosovar Albanians who illegally immigrated into Serb is quite a different, and that's what we're discussing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question relates to Kosovar Albanians and the answer may be so confined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point, I think, should be taken from the context of the document that we've been looking at, which talks about "the Siptars making our job easier. They boycotted the census." It doesn't say "illegal immigrants." Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it says that they're not our citizens. Isn't that right, Mr. Bonomy? Otherwise, as far as the last question asked by Mr. Nice, I haven't forgotten it. The Serbian Radical Party, as far as I remember, had another document which had to do -- which was related to Kosovo and Metohija, and that was in September 1995, I believe. We published a memorandum about our vision of the way in which to solve the Kosovo and Metohija problem, and that was compiled by a working group on behalf of the Serbian Radical Party and was signed by the whole leadership of the party. It signed that memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will remember tab 30 of the witness's own exhibits, which is the speech given in March 1999 in Belgrade. And I don't have the bundle from which the witness was reading, and I don't remember whether he had a version of this in his own language. The Chamber will remember that the passage upon which we focussed was at page 5 in the English text, at the top. The witness will need a copy of the document. We've got one for him. Or if the accused or the assigned counsel have whatever he was reading at the time. Ms. Dicklich, as ever, has found one. This is several years later, 1999. We'll just play it on Sanction, please, for the audiovisual booth. Let's play the short extract that we have of this speech. We don't have all of it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "If it comes to bombing by the NATO pact, if it comes to an American aggression, we Serbs will suffer significant casualties, but there will be no more Albanians in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you'll remember being asked by the accused about that passage, and you took us --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you now have the text in front of you, which we have on English page 5, you sought to explain to us how and why it would be that there would be no Albanians in Kosovo. And I'd like you, in a calm voice, please, to find us whereabouts in this text the Albanians could interpret your words other than as words that would promise violence to them and forced expulsion, at the least.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right in the previous paragraph, and I'll read it out to you: "We Serbs are a peoples with democratic traditions. We are divided ideologically, politically in different ways. But when it comes to the fatherland, there is no division. Let us see which Serb can sign an agreement for foreign troops to come onto our territory. Let us see which Serb is ready to sign the separation of Kosovo and Metohija from the legal system of Serbia. We, the Serbs, as a democratic nation, have many times offered to the Albanians the highest degree of autonomy, cultural autonomy, for them to live as loyal citizens, for them themselves to be able to regulate their health system, education system, information system, et cetera. But they do not want to. All they want is secession, and to secede they will not be able to do that alone. They are conscious of that so they count upon the Americans, that the Americans will fight their battle for them in the Balkans from this position. I would like to tell them, and this isn't a message of the Serbian Radical Party alone, I am convinced it is a message from the entire Serb people: The Albanians will have a chance only if they orient themselves towards a peaceful, democratic, political road of dialogue." And then the quotation that you showed us a moment ago. I can read that out too again, if you so desire. "If there is bombing ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have the reference on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you read -- read the quotation, but then read the next couple of sentences on the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "If there is bombing, in the event of a NATO bombing, in the event of an American aggression, we Serbs shall perish in quite large numbers, but there will be no Albanians in Kosovo. Surely the Americans do not believe that if they attack us, we will allow armed bands and disloyal citizens behind our backs who can hardly wait to stab us in the back. We will not allow that, and let them see what to do with them afterwards."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Take us to any other passage that you want to. Why would there, on the passage we've looked at, why would there be no Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an American aggression comes about, and bombing, then they will suffer first and then the Serbs too. Secondly, we have the experience of the bombing of Republika Srpska with depleted uranium. You now have occasions of Albanian children born with two heads and other genetic deformities. Third, I state that we won't allow any armed bands to stab us in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We had all that material before, but I'm just trying to see how a Kosovar Albanian, hearing what you say, would have any other impression than that they were about to be kicked out. Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I tell them that the Albanians have a chance only if they opt for a peaceful, democratic, political way of dialogue. Otherwise, there will be war, and war brings suffering and destruction to everyone. And mostly to them in Kosovo and Metohija. I assume that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, with that answer, we take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we went from 1991 to 1999 for reasons of Kosovo collection. I'm going to go back to 1992. And a general point I want to make to you and through you is this, that -- and we're only interested in not in your case, we're interested in the society in which you were operating and what you were allowed to do. And the position is that you were allowed to instil hate through messages of what would happen to other ethnic groups right through this period of time. That's the proposition, so that you can know what we're looking at. I want to look at three or four exhibits, very quickly, for want of time. For the interpreters, the first one will be 23g -- I'm so sorry. Before I move on, I hadn't asked for admission of the latest exhibit before we turned to tab 30 in the witness's bundle. That's the second extract from Ustasha Phantasmagorias. May it be given a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the interpreters' benefit, we now go to 23.g.3. In the English on the document coming your way, it's page 6 of 8. On the original, it's page 174 and 175.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, Mr. Seselj, was a speech in Belgrade, speech of the deputies. So this is in parliament, I think, or the Assembly. And the first extract reads as follows. It's on page 6. "Let me reiterate: We are going to expel the Croats --" Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "We are going to expel the Croats, exercising the same right that Tudjman has exercised to expel the Serbs. You can do your research in Zagreb and find out what this right was, since you have not yet raised a single voice of protest against Tudjman's crimes, against the expulsion of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbs and everything else that is happening on the territory of Ustasha Croatia, primarily genocide against the Serbian people. We are not going to resort to genocidal activities, because it is not in the blood of us Serbs. We are not going to start killing you, of course. We are simply going to pack you into trucks and trains and let you manage in Zagreb." And then the passage about giving address of abandoned Serbs homes. If you turn to the second passage on the 7th of April, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why don't you read that, Mr. Nice? Read everything that's being marked, or let me read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second passage. You can -- I'm just going to ask you the question, then you can deal with it as swiftly as possible. 7th of April, 1992, at page 7: "Ladies and gentlemen, people's deputies, this storm in a teacup following my personal demand, which was also the Serbian Radical Party's demand, to exercise retaliation measures and let the Croats move out of Serbia, because of the fact that a great number of Serbs has been forced to move out, has only strengthened my belief that the demand is fully correct. "The mere fact that the fiercest reactions to it have come from the traitor-like political parties in the Serbian public, only strengthens my determination, and as for those traitor-like political parties and their leaders, such as one of their representatives who spoke here just now, perhaps the best solution - if they pity the Croats so much - would be simply putting them on buses and trucks and taking them to Zagreb." Now, here in the Assembly, twice, clear indication of forced transportation of Croats. Is that correct? That's the sort of thing you were allowed to say and did say?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was not "allowed" anything. It was my right to say it. And no one could deny me that right. I was speaking here as a deputy. But because your interpretation is incorrect, I will read out both passages in their entirety, if the Chamber does not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Time is limited. Can you explain the error, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, just concentrate on what you think was omitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the first passage, Mr. Nice, although it's marked here in the document, he read out my message to the Croats. He omitted the following: "You will even get the addresses of abandoned Serbian homes, houses, flats. You can move into those. The furniture has been left there too, and you can take from here whatever you like, everything you need." Mr. Nice omitted to read this on purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that gives it a different slant? Do you say that that omission, the words omitted which you have just read, gives it a different slant? If so, what is that perspective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because when Tudjman was expelling the Serbs, several hundred thousand Serbs, he did not allow them to take their basic necessities with them. They left their houses with the furniture inside and all their belongings. However, although advocating retortion, I said that they could take with them whatever they wanted. This went on for a few months. Serbia was overwhelmed by a wave of Serb refugees and expelled Serbs. The Serb Radical Party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where were you at, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He wanted to correct some translation point on one of the other sections and I've asked him to deal with it quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's the other translation point you want to say, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You omitted to read, when I'm telling the Serbian traitors to go to Zagreb, the following: "There they have democracy. There they will live a good life. What can they expect here in Serbia? The standpoint of the Serbian people is evident, and the enthusiasm with which they met this proposal." I'm addressing the Serb traitors now. "What do they want with the Serbia which doesn't understand them? Go to Tudjman." So this is really my settling of accounts with the opposing parties at the rostrum. The facts are that the Serb Radical Party was in favour of the principle of retortion. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does "retortion" mean forced removal, which was the question you were asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Retortion means retaliation. If Tudjman expelled the Serbs, then Serbia should expel the Croats. That's retortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's your view, is it? You're espousing -- no matter how innocent the people might be living in Serbia, they should just be forced out because of the conduct of Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, that is the standpoint of the Serb Radical Party, and it is limited to a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm confirming what actually happened, because I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A number for this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite rapidly the next one, just to highlight the same point, short extract, 23f.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another thing that's important here, if I may say so. May I, Mr. Robinson? I am speaking here as a member of parliament of the opposition of the Serb Radical Party, and no one can either permit me or prohibit me from saying this in the National Assembly. Because I see what Mr. Nice is trying to imply, that I was allowed to say this by Mr. Milosevic. But what can he have to do with it? If this is illegal behaviour, then it's my illegal behaviour and the illegal behaviour of my party. It has nothing whatsoever to do with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I was going to ask you to clarify that, so far as your case is concerned. Are you asking the Chamber to draw an inference from these speeches made by the witness, in parliament and outside, espousing the forcible removal of Croats, are you asking us to draw the inference that the same sentiments were held by members of the joint criminal enterprise, including Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That may well be an inference we'll invite you to draw, but at the moment, and through this witness, I'm restricting my questions somewhat to the proposition that he was in a culture where he was permitted to say these things by the authorities, and we've gone into the ups and downs of his relationships with the accused, and where he and indeed the accused would know that the permission to say these things creates the circumstances in which these offences would be committed. And may I remind the Chamber of the evidence we had from Mr. Zwaan about the mechanisms of genocidal-type crimes. So that there are two significances: Putting it at its lowest, it's that this material was regularly available in the regime operated by this accused, and that's extremely important in itself. The next upstage of inference is something we may invite you to draw separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will have to consider that carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On this particular occasion, he is rebuked by the chairman of the Assembly for what he is saying, because what he is saying is contrary to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. May we look next at this short extract from "Politics as a Challenge of Conscience," published in I'm not quite sure when. But the interview is the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you have that, Mr. Seselj, just the short passage that's got a mark down the side of it. You gave this speech: "I would expel the Croats for several reasons. First and foremost, because the Croats are extremely disloyal as inhabitants of Serbia, because the vast majority of them are members of the HDZ or act as foreign collaborators, and that they're doing everything they can to destabilise the internal situation in Serbia. In addition to that, the Croats have proved to be direct collaborators of the Ustasha, they made possible the transfer thereof from Vukovar to Hungary via Backa. Furthermore, we must apply the measures of retaliation against the Croats because Tudjman has expelled 160.000 Serbs." The only question I want to ask you about this passage is this: Here you seem to be referring, without distinct or discrimination, to all the Croats. And this book was published in Belgrade in 1993.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not referring to all the Croats, only those Croats who live in Serbia. And I am describing the characteristics of these Croats whom I wish to have expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any Croat living in Serbia and attending to this speech who --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen. -- would understand you to be saying that you would expel the Croats, just generally? As it reads, Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's agreed. He's agreed with your proposition. The Croats that live in Serbia should all be expelled. That's what he's just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can this be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying here is, you see, what you didn't read out: "We have to apply measures of retortion toward the Croats because Tudjman has expelled 160.000 Serbs." I go on to say: "That's the number officially registered, although we assume the number is twice as large, because many Serbs have not registered as refugees but are staying with friends and relatives. Also, many Serbs have fled from Croatia to third countries, and these Serbs have to be given accommodation, jobs, and they have to be provided for. We don't have enough money to build new residential buildings, factories, workplaces, and so on."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 912.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next one, a short video, 23.g.2, for the interpreters. Now concerned with Hrtkovci in Vojvodina, from which people believing themselves to be Croats left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Mr. Seselj, that those people who believed themselves to be Croats left after a speech of yours on the 6th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single Croat was expelled from Serbia. A certain number of Croats did leave, but all of them previously exchanged their property with Serbs who had been expelled, through the courts. And the Roman Catholic Church mediated in this exchange of property. Through their channels they would first establish whether the abandoned Serbian property in Croatia was intact, and only if it was would an exchange contract be signed. My attitude is one thing, and the fact that no one was expelled from Serbia is another thing. But that I advocated the principle of retortion, that is a fact, in response to what the Tudjman's regime was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You read the names, some of those who had to go, and here's your explanation on the television for what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... they're lying, and I will prove they are lying. In Hrtkovci, I did not call out the names of Croats ... from Hrtkovci who went to Croatia and were serving in the Ustasha National Guard Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm just going to start this again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Another thing, regarding what is in the indictment, they are lying and I will prove they are lying. In Hrtkovci, I did not call out the names of Croats who should be expelled, but I read a list of Croats from Hrtkovci who went to Croatia and were serving in the Ustasha National Guard Corps. There were no expulsions, and regarding my statements, I was not making them as someone from the government, but as someone from the opposition."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you reading out those names, whoever they were, to encourage others to leave?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never read out any names, but the activists of the Serb Radical Party who spoke at the meeting before me read out a few names of Croats who had left Hrtkovci to go to Croatia and become members of the National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said you read out a list of names, unless I misunderstood it. Did you or did you not read out a list of names?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you so impatient? It wasn't I who read it out. A member of my party did. But it comes down to the same thing, because I was standing next to him when he was reading them out. I don't have time to go into details here when I'm explaining things. But I do stand behind that list. It was read out by a member of my party who was standing next to me. We have a video of the rally in Hrtkovci, and I published the entire contents in the book "The Devil's Apprentice, the Criminal Pope John Paul II." Your colleague had the book in her hands, because I handed it over to the Trial Chamber on another occasion. So she has the whole contents of that rally. And when a member of my party read out that list, it comes to the same thing as if I had read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Seselj. We have the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So what was the likely consequence of reading those names out, then? That people would stay there or that they'd leave?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But these people had already left, whose names were read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell me this: Was it supposed to be done in a civilised way, this removal of people from Hrtkovci, on your interpretation of the word "civilised"? Was it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm surprised you haven't got this text, or a video of that rally, and then we could discuss specific facts. This was a pre-election rally. I was promising what we would do if we came to power. We will give those Serbs who had fled the addresses of Croats so that they can apply to them and say: Our property is over there, yours is over here, let's exchange it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed, what happened to those who didn't want to exchange? They'd have to go in any case? The border was going to be closed, that sort of thing. Did they have to go?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody left without previously exchanging their property and having the exchange registered by the court. And regularly, the Croats from Serbia got hold of property of a greater value than the property they left. There is not a single Croat you can name who was expelled from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that one be exhibited. And then I just have one more on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you now, please, Mr. Seselj, look at this extract, 23.g.3.4. It's a longer extract. I'm only going to take a short part of it. Re-examination can take more, if necessary. But this comes from a book of yours. And on your page 701, we can see the extract. If you go over, please, to page 280 - sorry - in your text, we see, and this is speaking about Hrtkovci, a civilised exchange of population, you said this: "It was supposed to be done in a more civilised way than it was actually carried out, but in any case, we are satisfied with the results. Thousands of Serbian families were accommodated in some extent, they were given houses and apartments in Hrtkovci (present-day Srbislavci)." What was it that was less civilised than planned? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were incidents here and there, because a large mass of Serbian refugees arrived in Serbia, most of them in Vojvodina. They turned up in large numbers in places where Croats lived. There was sporadic incidents that occurred, which we condemned and which we did not accept. But in a heated atmosphere, it was impossible to avoid them. Mr. Nice, I would like everything that you marked to be read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... warmed up the atmosphere if it wasn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not warm up an atmosphere that would create incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you or did you not turn up the temperature by your inflammatory speeches? Please help us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not heat up incidents. What we advocated was for the Serbs expelled from Croatia to exchange their property with the Croats from Serbia. You can see that in all of my speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were a few incidents where the police intervened, and the perpetrators were convicted. I know of two cases where perpetrators were convicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be 914.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move now not to Srebrenica 1993 but to Srebrenica 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Remind us, please, your position in society in 1995. What were you doing then?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995? In 1995 I was a convict, under the government of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: New Year's found me in prison. I was there for a total of four months. I was released on the 9th of January. And on the 3rd of June, I was arrested again, in Gnjilane, with my closest collaborators, and spent another two months in gaol.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you have told us all -- not all that you know, but you've told us what you say you know about events at Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As deputy Prime Minister later on, you worked on the issue intensively, correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you told us already --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us already only a thousand people killed. I say "only" a thousand people killed, and the French intelligence behind it. I think I asked you last week whether you could point us to any documents, that is original documents, and the answer, I think, is that you couldn't; correct? Original documents to support your suggestion about the French intelligence involved --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can, Mr. Nice. I can't show you the document, but I can tell you where you can find it: In the Dutch parliament. A document was submitted in which, according to the estimation of the Dutch officers, it is said that about a thousand Muslim prisoners of war were executed. That was the official information I received as deputy Prime Minister from our competent services. But I don't have this document in my hands now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, please, as deputy Prime Minister, apart from that document that you've identified now, tell us, please, what were the inquiries that were made into Srebrenica, as you understand it; starting when, by whom they were made, what reports they generated.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about the work of the investigating organs. You have seen a document here relating to Erdemovic. What I can tell you is what I personally, on my own initiative, did, as the deputy Prime Minister, and what I did before I became deputy Prime Minister, in order to learn, in as much detail as possible, about the events in Srebrenica. As deputy Prime Minister in charge of the economy and finances, I was not in charge of the judiciary. That was not my portfolio, so I could not go into its work directly. However, as deputy Prime Minister, I did everything I could to learn as many details as possible about the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is what you told us before, but I actually want an answer to my question, first of all, and then I might ask you another question about the answer you've given, or the things you've said. It's not an answer. What inquiries were made into Srebrenica at the time? When, by whom, what reports were generated? A simple question for a man in government. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As deputy Prime Minister, I was informed by the State Security Service about its efforts to learn the full truth about Srebrenica. In the government, we had a regular system of informing the Prime Minister and deputy Prime Ministers. We had daily information, periodic information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Seselj. Hold your horses, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. as they say. Steady on. You were informed by the state security about its efforts to learn the full truth. Right. What were the State Security Service's efforts to learn the full truth, and what reports did it generate, if any?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the efforts were and what they did is something that the State Security Service did not inform us of. These daily reports were one to three pages long, about different events. Sometimes the sources were under code and sometimes the source was general information. I cannot go into the methodology used by the State Security Service to gain information. However, I was informed of the results by that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why can't you go into the methodology and tell us what they did? If you want to tell this Court --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know that? Mr. Nice, we received these reports from the SDB unsigned, and they were marked "strictly confidential" and they were under seal. They were in a closed envelope and we were told to send them back as soon as we'd read them, on the same day.
