These reports were not kept in the government offices, they were sent back by courier on the same day. You don't imagine that the State Security Service was free with its information, giving it to all and sundry in the government. How could it survive if it had done that? How could it have survived as a service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... or at least place it on the overhead projector, which is I think what we're going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document from the Office of the Prosecutor, where we have requested -- it's in English. It has to be in English. We've requested the government of Serbia and Montenegro, in November 1993, after you were surrendered here, to supply all documentation and reports and memoranda, whenever prepared, which refer to the situation in and around Srebrenica between the 1st of April and the 31st of December, 1995, including and originating from the General Staff of the army; the federal Ministry of Defence; army intelligence; RDB and RJB of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. On your evidence, if there were any intelligence reports prepared in relation to Srebrenica, they should have been provided pursuant to that Request For Assistance, shouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Nice, I'm not quite clear on who I was turned over to. You say I was turned over to someone. Who to? That's the first point. Now, the second point is: These documents of the State Security Service existed at the time when I was vice-premier. What their fate was after that, I don't know. I know about just one piece of information, and that is that a vast quantity of documents belonging to the State Security Service after the 5th of October 2000, was burnt, in the Institute for Security in Belgrade. That news reached me. Now, what was burnt and how it was burnt, how would you expect me to know that? And today, in power, are your people in Serbia, the people you like. So how come they won't do you a favour? I can't answer this question, because people who are your bosses put people in power in Serbia and they don't want to comply with your requests. What do I have -- do I have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... answer to the question, please. If your evidence is correct, and subject to what you've said about it all being burnt and destroyed, the evidence is correct, if your evidence is correct, this document should have brought forth some reports, shouldn't it? Because you're saying that you saw reports that enabled you to come to this Court, and on the solemn declaration, told the Judges that, apart from the thousand prisoners of war who died as a result of the behaviour of one sabotage detachment, nothing else happened, and what did happen was a result of the French. So there should be some material, shouldn't there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would that have to mean that? Had I, on the 17th of November, 2003, by any chance been president of the federal government and had I received this letter from you, I would have responded and told you that we didn't want to cooperate with you and weren't going to supply you with anything. That would have been my answer to you had I been the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you've presented a version of events at Srebrenica. It's important, I think, that we consider absolutely everything we can lay our hands on that might support that version of events. And what the Prosecutor is trying to do is identify what exists, what material exists to support that. Now, do you not also see it as in everyone's interest connected with the former Yugoslavia to present material which might support that version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bonomy. However, he's asking me the wrong questions. They are more provocations and make me defiant rather than get an answer from me. If he doubts that I had the documents in my hand, then he should say so, say that he doubts that. If he believes that I have those documents in my hands, then I can talk, to the best of my recollections, talk about the contents of some of those documents, but I can't jump out of my own skin and explain why the federal government failed to send him anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's trying to refine the material, and I have to express concern about the answer you gave, that if you had received that document, which is in standard terminology, you would have said that you didn't want to cooperate and you weren't going to supply anything. What sort of attitude is that for a responsible politician to take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the conditional, Mr. Bonomy. Had I been president of the federal government at that point in time. That was the condition. Then my stand would be that this Tribunal was illegal and that I don't want to cooperate with them. Had I been present. But unfortunately, I wasn't Prime Minister. So that's one position. Let's leave that aside for the moment and look at the second point. I say that our services, security services, dealt with the problem in Srebrenica and that they investigated what exactly happened in Srebrenica. That's what I assert. You can believe me or not believe me. What can I do? I can't change my position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But is there nothing you can point us to that we can perhaps put our hands on that will support the account you've given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, you can check this out in Serbia. You have sufficient resources. The Prosecution has sufficient resources and agents of its own, so you can check out and see whether the security service and, to a very small circle of top-ranking officials, sent daily reports about various information that it came by. That is something that can be investigated, checked out. This type of communication did in fact exist. Then there were periodical reports, and from time to time we would receive from the military intelligence certain reports if they considered it to be important for the government of Serbia as well. And that's how we received information about the fact that Momcilo Perisic and Jovica Stanisic were recruited to work from the CIA. We received that from the army, a report to that effect, from the military intelligence. I don't know if it's true or not. But I had in my hands a piece of paper and read it. On the basis of that, we decided to dismiss and replace Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not really discussing that at the moment, Mr. Seselj. We have your account and we have a note -- or I note well the material you say that account is founded on. It's to see if there is anything else that is actually tangible that can be -- hands can be laid upon. And it seems that your answer is you don't know of the existence of any such material. And I take it - and this is a question - I take it that there never was a transparent inquiry in Serbia into the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, pursuant to the laws of Serbia, an investigation is conducted by the court, and the police services - the civilian police, the military police, the secret service and so on and so forth - what they deal with is the gathering of information. The gathering of information is not an investigation. That information has different degrees of reliability. Sometimes you say the source is reliable. Then they tell us that the source is relatively reliable. Sometimes unreliable. Sometimes reliable, sometimes not reliable, partially reliable, partially unreliable. Those are the different degrees and qualifications of each piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But my understanding is that the investigation having been carried out, at a later stage there was a change of face and a decision to release people that you say were involved. So there's never been a sort of open and public examination of the issue in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An investigation was launched officially when we had something in our hands, and we had the suspects, like Pelemic, Petrusic and so on. Five of them, I think there were, five suspects. I can't remember now. Then the investigation was launched sometime at the beginning of the year 2000, if I remember correctly. That's when we had something tangible in our hands. The investigation is a highly complex one. Some knowledge and information was made public. Mr. Nice here has confirmation that I spoke about that far earlier than the federal minister did about those things. Not all the details, but some points. He can see that from those books here. Now, we are conducting the investigation and we want to bring it to an end and have a complete investigation and to prosecute the authorities, change -- there's a putsch, a coup d'etat, these people are suddenly released from prison and symbolic sentences are meted out to them just for the time they spent in prison so the government did not have to pay remuneration to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't mean you just to repeat what you've said. I fully understand that. That's all I need to ask, Mr. Nice..

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the Request For Assistance be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now distribute the next document, which is, for the booth, it's 120, tab 120. And it comes with documents attached. This is their response, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia and Montenegro. And it lists nine documents, a report from the 1st Army Command, second report from the 1st Army Command, periodic report from the 2nd Army Command, a report from the Uzice Corps, information from the VJ General Staff administration, periodic report from the 2nd Army Command, daily report from the 10th Counter-intelligence Group, document from the VJ administration, document from the VJ administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've got the documents there if you want to look at them. I don't want to take the time now. And we have the index. Is any of these the document or a document on which you relied when you told the learned Judges what your account of Srebrenica is?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that there were any of these documents, because what we received were not reports of this nature. What we received was processed information, which means information -- it's like this: We would get two pieces of paper, for example, or three pieces of paper, and then on half a page you would have one process or a recap of a piece of information. The next page would be a piece of information on quite a different matter, and so on and so forth. But we never received any military documents of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is this request in November 2003 the first request the Prosecution made for this material?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't say whether it's the first request of that kind, I can check that, but it's the first request signed in this series of requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, were you not in a position to make these inquiries much earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think there are much earlier paper trails in which there was further detailed requests. If you look at the next response to this - can we have 121, please, tab 121. Thank you very much. I'm sorry, can the last one be admitted. It's the only documents that have been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the basis for admitting this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two bases, really. First of all, documents, I think, from governments may be produced without the technicality of an identifying witness from time to time, and helpfully. And indeed, as part of that first answer to Your Honour's question, our inquiry is indeed the inquiry that His Honour Judge Bonomy, namely we simply want to find out through the witness by reference to other inquiries we've made what it is said is available. The second part is that the witness has said he was shown certain documents. We are trying to find out through his various answers what documents he maintains existed that enabled him to form an opinion. He's now looked at this index, he hasn't looked at all the documents, but expressed the provisional view that these are not they. That's, therefore, quite significant and important. Indeed it founds, no doubt, the possibility of further application for further documents. But as it stands, it's part of the general exercise to see what it has been said exists in relation to this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand the second part of the answer, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The authorities have produced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he says that these are not the documents, how then does that become some kind of a basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, it identifies -- I suppose it further identifies the category of documents upon which he says he is relying. It also shows that he didn't rely on these documents insofar as they contain anything even potentially relevant. It's all part of presenting to you through this witness, as we're entitled, indeed sensibly obliged to do, the picture which we will in due course argue, absent further provision, that either nothing helpful or explanatory existed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand what you're trying to do. It's just that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Defence would oppose --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, this witness was in custody when this request was sent here, so I don't see how he can take this any further at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's surely impossible to understand the answer to the question unless you have this document there. It's not one of these documents that is going to be used in some sense to test credibility, reliability, or supplement the Prosecution case. It simply enables us to see that when a request was made, and it was answered - and I take it you accept that this is the answer that's been presented by a responsible prosecutor - that when the answer was given, it didn't include anything that the witness has been referring to. And that seems to -- it seems to be necessary to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't think it's something that he can help at all upon in relation to this. It's to the government of which he was not a member of in relation to this particular government at this time. It's material arising after he's in custody here. Surely we're better off dealing with more relevant and pertinent material arising from the time when he had any kind of responsibility or authority to deal with any kind of request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The material sent from Belgrade at the request of Mr. Nice is from material which originate from military archives. And what Mr. Nice says, that there's nothing here that would be potentially relevant about Srebrenica, is not true, is not correct, because in this document there are several documents within this one. You have the report by the command of the 1st Army, for instance, which comprises all the areas, then the border towards Republika Srpska Krajina, then towards Republika Srpska, which lists the activities of the Monitoring Mission, the United Nations, Alpha [phoen], and so on, and everything else that was happening. But that is 1995, and the month is April. After that -- this is a voluminous document, a regular military document. After that, you have the 7th of July, for instance, where certain reports are also shown. And what can be seen from our territory, some shells fell on our territory, and so on and so forth. And here we can see from this that our authorities didn't have an insight at all into what was happening across the border, and that the reports report about what is happening on our side. Because certain shells seemed to be falling on our side. So had they had an insight and knew what was going on across the border, they would have written that down. That's why it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do I understand you, then, that you would have no objection to admission of this document? Because it contains relevant --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection to admission of this document. Take a look at this, Mr. Robinson, please. You have the command of the 2nd Army, for example, on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it then, on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I complete this short part of the paper trail.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 916.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the next one, please, which is Supplementary Request For Assistance, tab 121, for the interpreters. And if we can distribute that. It's already been distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, you'll discover, on reading, Mr. Seselj, notes the earlier response, observes that the initial request was sufficiently broad to cover a number of state institutions. It goes on to say that: "In order to provide the Trial Chamber with a full and proper account of efforts made by the Office of the Prosecutor to secure relevant and probative evidence for the above-mentioned Prosecution, and to leave a transparent record of the efforts undertaken by the Office of the Prosecutor ... the Prosecution seeks an explanation as to the steps taken fully to comply with the original Request ... and to state the names of the institutions canvassed and comprehensively document in writing the steps taken." If we can just have that there and then turn, please, to the last of these documents, which is tab 122, for the interpreters. The response came on the 4th of November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document, dated the 4th of November, notes the supplementary request and says in the second paragraph that: "Acting upon the request from the OTP, it's forwarded the subject request to Ministry of Defence of Serbia and Montenegro, Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, and has received replies from the named authorities that they have no other knowledge of the events related to Srebrenica except that which has already been provided." It goes on to say that: "The Srebrenica Commission of the Republika Srpska government has applied to Serbia and Montenegro with a similar request, and in response to this, the ministry has requested subject documentation from a wider circle of institutions. The reply received consisted only of the documentation we had already received, provided to the OTP." So what it comes down to is that the nine documents originally provided, Mr. Seselj, are all that the authorities have provided us. And there's one other point beyond those points that I was making to the learned Judges when they asked me for the relevance of this material, and it's a point that I should have made earlier, and I'm obliged to Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff to ensure that I'm making it now. Is the proper inference that the Judges should draw from the fact that this nine documents are the only documents that were provided, that your account of there being other documents is simply not true? Do you see what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see what you're saying. Perhaps they don't exist any more. But I claim that I had in my hands several different types of documents in which our security services deal with the question of Srebrenica. Whether they exist today or not is another matter. That there were daily reports, that there were periodical reports, that there were analytical reports, that is to say an analysis of the overall event, that is a fact. Now, if they no longer exist, if Vuk Draskovic tells you, as the minister, that they don't exist any more, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May those two documents be exhibited, on the same basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've got one short topic to deal with, with your leave, before we break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider this overnight, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A short point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just look at that photograph from the ... I'm going to show you -- put on the overhead projector a still from the Skorpions video, Mr. Seselj. Just look at it, please. That's a still from the video that it is said shows young men being taken from an area near Trnovo, originating from Srebrenica, to be executed. Can you now, please, look at this document, which is one of your filings to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can that go on the overhead projector and he have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is what you said to this Court, Mr. Seselj, in respect of that video. You spoke of Natasa Kandic and you said: "She is also known to the Trial Chamber as the person who submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor the rigged 12-minute film with scenes of people being shot, allegedly in the vicinity of Trnovo, represented as if they related to Srebrenica. If the footage had been shown in full, one would have seen how the supposed victims stand up and their hands are untied. The Office of the Prosecutor has not shown the footage in full deliberately, even though it knows well that this is doctored footage shot by two cameramen on the basis of a special film script. The Office of the Prosecutor is aware of this doctoring as it is in the possession of the complete footage, which is precisely why it has not requested that it be included in the evidence, as this would expose the fraud." Mr. Seselj, of those men walking up that hill, three at least have been identified by their relations. Would you now please tell us on what basis you say that film, which was screened extensively in Serbia, is a fraud. What's your knowledge and evidence for making that assertion in relation to these people whose bereaved families have been able to identify their sons?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this was prepared by the expert team helping in my Defence. I signed the document that they sent me from Belgrade. The object of this document -- just wait a minute, please, so that I can explain what this is about. I'm not giving up. I'm not not going to answer. Let's see what this is about first. This is my submission informing the Prosecution, in conformity with Rule 67 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, of the intention to present a separate defence, a special defence. And in my submission, I am trying to disqualify one of the witnesses who was not a protected witness, by the way, Dr. Zoran Stankovic, general and former head of the VMA, Medical Military Academy. There's no need for me not to mention his name because he's not a protected witness. So I charged my expert team to find testimony and evidence which morally discredit him as your potential witness. My team members came to the -- came by the information that this video was rigged. On the basis of what? I'll tell you. Who would be as stupid as have a group of Muslims captured in Srebrenica, driven to Trnovo, almost 200 kilometres away from Srebrenica, and then to execute them there and then to film their execution? Do you know where Trnovo is? Trnovo is right the other side of Sarajevo. To get to Trnovo from Srebrenica you have to go to Bratunac first, then Vlasenica, then Han Pijesak, then Sokolac, then to Pale and right across the Trebevic mountain by roundabout way to Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've given you, as is customary, time for putting the matter in context. Please answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What is your knowledge and evidence for making the assertion that this film is rigged, a forgery?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of my expert team have proof and evidence, and I shall present them to the Prosecution once I receive them. Because they didn't write this off the top of their head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it your case, then, that these young men shown in this film are still alive and is that what you want people to believe?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I cannot know that. But I am asserting that the filming of the execution was improvised. That's what I am stating and claiming, and that that was done for somebody's propaganda needs. That's what I'm claiming too. And thirdly, I still do not have a privileged television communication with my legal advisors and members of the expert team for the preparation of my defence. I still cannot have confidential conversations with them, so I have not been provided with many pieces of information. Perhaps they have this complete footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what's the date on the submission, the filing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's September 8th of this year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The 29th of August this year. And this was sent me in the month of July. And as I was blocked, contrary to the war, the post wasn't -- I didn't receive any post for two months, and this arrived in The Hague in the course of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to ask him two questions, if I may, which -- I'll identify the questions and the Court can decide if they can go to the witness. One is can he identify the evidence and make it available to us tomorrow or tell us how he can get it. And the second thing is: Does he have, so that we can see it, a video of his speech at Hrtkovci? Again, it would be helpful, if he has it here in The Hague, if he could bring that with him tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will -- the videotape of my speech in Hrtkovci I do not have here with me. Members of my expert team do have it in Belgrade, however. Here I have the integral text of the rally published in the book "The Devil's Apprentice, the Criminal Pope John Paul II." And a few days ago, I handed over similar document to the Prosecution in which I deal with the case of Natasa Kandic and her amassment of false indictments against and accusations against the Serbs. And there is a series of pieces of evidence there, and in that context you can view the question of this videotape which she allegedly arrived by and how she arrived by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now and resume tomorrow, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of September, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
